public.title: How Computers Work
public.goal: Understand a computer from the transistor to the web page: what's inside it, how it stores anything, how it runs a program, how it starts, and how it talks to the world. No earlier knowledge is assumed.

project.title: Explain your own laptop

blocks.text: Write a clear report about your own laptop, so that someone with no computing background could follow it. Use real readings. Keep private details out: no account name, addresses, passwords or file names.
Your report needs these five parts.

items: **What's inside.** A specification table from real readings, covering the processor, cores, RAM, drive type and capacity, graphics and ports. Say what each part does.

**How your data is stored.** Choose one real file of each kind: text, a picture, and audio or video. Give its size. Calculate its uncompressed size, where you can. Say whether it's compressed, and whether that compression is lossy.
**What happens in one click.** Your own trace of opening a web page, from the touchpad to the pixels, from `hcw-one-click`, including what you really observed in the browser's developer tools.

**What could go wrong.** Pick three real risks to this laptop. For each, say which part of the machine it involves, and whether it harms confidentiality, integrity or availability. Say what protects you now, and what you'd change.

**What you changed.** Describe at least one real improvement you made because of this course, such as a tested backup, a startup app you removed, or drive encryption you checked. Say how you confirmed that it worked.

blocks.text: Write it in your own words. Your own explanation is the point, so don't paste it from anywhere, and don't have an AI write it. This project is self-checked, and the app will record it that way.

rubric: All five parts are present, and they use real readings from this laptop.
I wrote it in my own words, and I could explain any sentence of it aloud.
It contains no private details.
I really made the improvement that I describe, and I checked that it worked.

lessons.pack: What a computer does
lessons.title: Follow information through a computer
lessons.source: GCFGlobal · Computer Basics
lessons.courses: UNIPORT (expected) COS 101, CSC 101 · NOUN COS101, GST103
lessons.lectureCredit: Code.org · What Makes a Computer, a Computer?
lessons.goal: Trace any task on a computer as input, processing, storage and output, and say which part of the machine does each job.
lessons.why: Every topic in both your degrees sits on this model. Programming is writing the processing step. Statistics is deciding what the input means. Cybersecurity is asking who can see or change the information at each stage. If you can trace information through a task, you always have somewhere to start, even on a machine or program you have never seen.

sections.title: The four things a computer does

blocks.text: Follow the four jobs as the presenters move from a button press to a result. Watch for an output that is not a screen image, such as a signal to a robot. The lesson below adds a worked Windows task and separates temporary memory from saved files.

A computer is a machine that follows stored instructions to work on information. Whatever it looks like, a phone, a laptop or a bank's server, it does four things. It takes **input**, it **processes** it, it **stores** it, and it gives **output**.

head: Stage
What happens
Examples
rows: Keys you press, a photo from the camera, a file being opened, data arriving from the internet
Instructions change or compare the information
Adding numbers, searching for a word, shrinking a photo
A saved document on the drive, a contact on your phone
Text on the screen, sound, a printed page, a message sent to another computer

blocks.text: Input does not have to come from a person, and output does not have to go to one. When your phone checks the time with a server, one computer's output is the other computer's input. This is how most of the world's computing happens.
Worked example: a calculator app
Suppose you type 12 + 30 and press equals.

items: **Input:** the keys 1, 2, +, 3, 0 and =.
**Processing:** the app turns those key presses into two numbers and an instruction to add them. The processor does the addition.
**Output:** 42 appears on the screen.
**Storage:** usually none that lasts. Close the app and the sum may be gone, unless the app keeps a history. To find out which, you test it.

blocks.question: Sending a WhatsApp message is one task made of many steps. Name one input, one piece of processing, one storage and one output.
blocks.answer: Input: the characters you type. Processing: the app encrypts the message and prepares it for sending. Storage: the chat history is written to your phone. Output: the encrypted message goes out over the network, and it appears on your screen. Other correct answers exist, so check yours by asking whether each one really fits its stage.

blocks.text: **Hardware** is the physical equipment you could touch: keyboard, screen, processor, memory, drive. **Software** is the instructions that tell the hardware what to do. A program is one set of instructions, such as a browser. The operating system, such as Windows, is the software that runs the machine and lets other programs share it.

Neither is useful alone. A processor with no instructions does nothing, and a program with no hardware cannot run. When something goes wrong, this split helps you think. If a key is physically broken, reinstalling a program will not fix it. If an app crashes on one file but others work, the screen is not the problem.
People often say "the computer" when they mean one program. If Chrome is frozen, Windows may be fine. Name the exact part you mean, because the fix depends on it.

A **trace** follows information step by step. Tracing is how programmers find bugs, how analysts check where a number came from, and how security people find weak points. Here is a trace of searching for a file in File Explorer.

head: Step
Stage
What actually happens
rows: You type `exam` in the search box
The characters reach File Explorer through Windows
Explorer reads the list of names from the drive
Saved information is copied into working memory
Matching files appear in the window
The output of the search becomes your next input

blocks.text: Notice that the last row starts the cycle again. Real tasks are chains, and the output of one step often becomes the input of the next.
How to tell whether something was stored

Do not guess. Run a small test. Do the task, close the program fully, and reopen it. If the result is still there, it was stored somewhere that lasts. A later lesson explains where. This habit of testing instead of assuming is the main idea of this whole course.

At each stage of a trace, ask three questions. Who should be able to **see** this? What happens if someone **changes** it? What happens if it is **lost or unavailable**? Those three questions come back later as confidentiality, integrity and availability.

Take paying someone by bank transfer. The account number you type is input, and someone watching your screen could read it. The bank's server processes the amount, and if that amount were changed, you would lose money. The bank stores the record, and if the server were down, you could not pay. One simple task raises all three questions, at different stages.
When you practise tracing, use your own tasks and your own devices. Tracing what your own computer does is always fine. Probing someone else's system is not, even out of curiosity.
Choose one task you really do on this laptop, such as opening a PDF, renaming a file, or searching for something.

items: Do the task once, slowly, and watch what happens.
Write one line for each stage: what was the input, what was processed, what was stored, what was the output.
Close the program fully and reopen it. Record what was still there and what was gone.
Pick one stage and answer the three security questions for it: see, change, lost.

blocks.text: Write in your own words. Keep private names out of your answer.

rubric: I traced a task I actually did, not an example from the lesson.
I tested what was stored by closing and reopening instead of guessing.
I answered the three security questions for at least one stage.

exercises.question: A voice note is recorded, sent, and played by a friend. On your phone, what is the input and what is the output?
exercises.answer: The input is the sound through the microphone. The output is the data sent over the network. On your friend's phone, that data is the input and the sound from the speaker is the output. The same data can be output for one device and input for another.

exercises.question: You edit a photo to make it brighter but do not save it, then close the app. Which of the four stages did not happen for the brighter version?
exercises.answer: Storage. It was input, processed and shown on the screen as output, but never kept. If the app autosaved, a copy was stored, and the way to know is to reopen it and look.

exercises.question: A printer prints the wrong page, yet the same document looks right on screen. Is this more likely a problem with the input or further along? Why?
exercises.answer: Further along. The screen shows the document was read and processed correctly, so the fault is later in the chain, such as the page settings or the printer. Tracing narrows down where to look.

summary: A computer takes input, processes it, stores it, and gives output.
Hardware is the physical equipment. Software is the instructions.
One step's output is often the next step's input, including between computers.
Test whether something was stored. Do not assume.
At each stage ask who can see it, what if it changes, and what if it is lost.

lessons.pack: Computing from the beginning
lessons.title: Where computers came from, and what the field is
lessons.source: Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Course page
lessons.goal: Tell the story of computing through its generations, describe a computer in terms of hardware, software and humanware, classify kinds of computers and software, and name the main areas and jobs in the field.
lessons.why: This is how COS 101 begins at both schools, and these topics are direct exam questions: generations of computers, who built what, types of computer and software. It also gives you a map. Over the coming years you'll study many separate topics, and it helps to see how they fit, and where your own direction, fraud, risk and security work, sits within the field.

blocks.text: A **computer** is an electronic machine that accepts data, processes it according to stored instructions, stores the results and produces output. The key word is **stored**: its instructions, called a **program**, are held inside the machine, so changing what it does only takes changing the program. That's what makes one machine able to do millions of different jobs.
**Data** are raw facts. **Information** is data processed into something meaningful. The scores 45, 72 and 60 are data. "The class average is 59" is information.

head: When
What
Why it matters
rows: Beads for doing arithmetic by hand
Punched cards controlling a weaving pattern, an early form of instructions
Designed with memory and a processing unit, though never completed. Babbage is often called the father of the computer
She published what's widely regarded as the first computer program, for that engine
Punched cards processed the US census. His firm later became part of IBM
A mathematical model of what can be computed at all

blocks.text: Early dates and "firsts" are argued over, and exam answers depend on your course material. Learn the version in your school's text.
Exams love this table. Each generation is named after the electronic technology it used.

head: Generation
Rough dates
Technology
Examples and features
rows: ENIAC, UNIVAC. Room-sized, hot and unreliable. Programmed in machine language
Smaller, cooler and more reliable. Assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL
Many transistors on one chip. Operating systems, keyboards and screens. IBM System/360
A whole processor on one chip. Personal computers, then laptops and phones
Systems that learn from data, and handle language and images

blocks.text: The trend throughout is smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable. **Moore's law**, Gordon Moore's observation, says the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled every two years for decades. It's an observed trend and not a law of nature, and it has slowed.

blocks.question: What was the key technology of the second generation, and what did it replace?
blocks.answer: The transistor, which replaced the vacuum tube, and which was smaller, cooler and more reliable.

blocks.text: A complete computer system has three parts, and COS 101 names all of them.

head: Part
What it is
Examples
rows: The people who build, run and use it

blocks.text: Basic parts of hardware

head: Unit
Job
Examples
rows: Carries out instructions. Its **control unit** directs, and its **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** calculates

blocks.text: **RAM** loses its contents without power, as a later lesson explains. **ROM**, read-only memory, keeps its contents, and holds startup instructions.
Kinds of software

head: Type
Purpose
Examples
rows: Does a job for the user

blocks.text: Kinds of computer

head: By size
Use
rows: Huge calculations, such as weather forecasting
Many users, large organisations, such as banks
Serving a department or a website
Personal use: desktops, laptops, tablets, phones

blocks.text: By data handling, a computer can be **analog** (continuous values), **digital** (discrete values), or **hybrid** (both). Nearly everything you use is digital.
"Computing" is really a family of disciplines. Nigeria's national standards group them, and your degrees touch several.

head: Area
Main question
Typical jobs
rows: How do computation and algorithms work?
How do we build reliable software?
How does technology serve an organisation?
How do we run technology for people?
How do we protect systems and data?
What can we learn from data?

blocks.text: Computing also shapes society. It changes how we bank, learn and vote, and it brings problems: fraud, privacy loss, automation of jobs and bias in automated decisions. Professionals are responsible for thinking about those.

Predictions tend to age badly, so hold these lightly. Current active areas include AI, cloud computing, the Internet of Things, and quantum computing, which is still early for most practical uses. The thing that lasts is the fundamentals, which is why your degrees spend four years on them.
Make your own study sheet, from memory first. Close this lesson for the first three steps.

items: Draw a timeline of the five generations, with the technology for each and one example. Then open the lesson, and correct it.
List the hardware units, with one example of each from this laptop. Find out this laptop's processor and amount of RAM: press Ctrl + Shift + Esc, and open Performance.
List six programs installed on your laptop, and classify each as system or application software.
From the table of areas, choose the two jobs that interest you most. Write one sentence on why, and which of your courses leads toward each.
Check your school's own COS101 or CSC 101 material, if you have it. Note anything that differs from this lesson. For the exam, your school's version wins.

rubric: I wrote the timeline from memory first, then corrected it.
I used real hardware and software from this laptop.
I connected two jobs to my own courses.

exercises.question: What's the difference between data and information? Give an example from school.
exercises.answer: Data are raw facts, such as each student's score. Information is the processed result, such as "60% passed".

exercises.question: Classify: Windows 11, Microsoft Word, a printer driver, a compiler.
exercises.answer: Windows 11 is system software. Word is application software. A driver is system software. A compiler is programming software.

exercises.question: Why did the transistor make such a difference over the vacuum tube?
exercises.answer: Transistors are much smaller, use less power, produce less heat and fail far less often.

exercises.question: Name the parts of a CPU, and what each does.
exercises.answer: The control unit directs the operations, and the arithmetic logic unit does calculations and comparisons.

summary: A computer accepts, processes, stores and outputs data, following a stored program.
Generations follow technology: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors, and AI.
A system is hardware, software and humanware.
Software is system, application or programming software.
Computing includes computer science, software engineering, information systems, IT, cybersecurity and data science.

lessons.pack: How Computers Work · What a computer is
lessons.title: The parts inside a computer
lessons.source: David J. Malan and Colton Ogden · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.lectureCredit: Harvard CS50 · David J. Malan, Colton Ogden
lessons.goal: Name the main parts inside a computer, say what each one does and how they connect, and read a laptop's real specification without being misled.
lessons.why: Once you know the parts, a computer stops being a magic box. You can buy the right laptop, tell what's worth repairing, and follow later lessons about how the processor and memory work. Security work needs this too: an investigator has to know where data can physically sit. You'll look at your own laptop's real parts in this lesson.

sections.title: A computer is a team of parts

blocks.text: David Malan and Colton Ogden look around a laptop's ports, then open up a desktop to show the real parts inside. It's a 2017 video, so some ports it shows, like the phone and DVD connectors, are rare today.
From the outside a laptop looks like one object. Inside, it's a team of separate parts, each with one job. Everything else in this course explains these parts in more depth.

head: Part
Its job
A simple comparison
rows: The large circuit board that connects everything
Holds what's in use right now
Keeps files with the power off
A worker who only does pictures
Removes heat, using a heat sink and often a fan

sections.title: The motherboard and how parts talk

blocks.text: A **circuit board** is a sheet carrying thin metal tracks that connect its components. The **motherboard** is the main one. The processor sits in or on it, memory plugs into it or is soldered to it, and storage connects to it. The tracks that carry data between parts are called a **bus**.
Worked example: opening a document
Follow one action across the parts:

items: You double-click. The **touchpad** sends a signal along the motherboard.
The **processor** runs instructions that work out what you clicked.
The document is read from **storage** and copied into **memory**.
The **processor** prepares it for display, often with the **graphics processor**.
The **screen** shows it.

blocks.text: Nothing happens in one place. Information moves between parts all the time.

Every part turns electricity into heat, and the processor produces the most. A **heat sink** is a block of metal with thin fins that spreads heat into the air, and a **fan** moves that air away. If the processor gets too hot, it slows itself down to protect itself. This is called **thermal throttling**. Don't block a laptop's vents with a pillow or bed, because it can make the laptop slower.

head: Desktop
Laptop
rows: Mains only, so a power cut stops it at once
Often limited, as memory may be soldered
Tight, so it gets hot more easily

blocks.text: Phones and many thin laptops use a **system on a chip** (SoC), which puts the processor, the graphics and more on one chip. That saves space and power, but you can't upgrade those parts separately.
**Ports** are the sockets where you connect things. **Peripherals** are the devices you attach.

head: Connection
Used for
rows: The classic rectangular port, for flash drives, mice and printers
The small oval port, often also used for charging and screens
Wired network, the "fat" cable shown in the clip
Short-range wireless for headphones and mice

blocks.text: A USB port carries data as well as power. An unknown flash drive can carry malware, and some charging points or cables can attempt data connections. Don't plug in a flash drive you found, and be careful with public charging points when you can use your own charger instead.
A **specification** lists what a computer has. Here's an example, and how to read it.

head: Listing says
It means
What to think
rows: The processor and how many tasks it can truly do at once
Generation matters too, so a new i5 can beat an old i7
Enough for several programs at once. 8 GB is a sensible minimum today
An SSD matters more for how fast it feels than a higher clock speed
Fine for study, weak for heavy 3D or AI work

blocks.text: Comparing laptops by clock speed alone. A 2.8 GHz chip isn't always faster than a 2.4 GHz chip. Design, generation and core count matter as much. Compare models by their real tests, not one number.

blocks.question: A listing says "1 TB memory". Is that RAM?
blocks.answer: Almost certainly not. It nearly always means storage. RAM on an ordinary laptop is far smaller, often 8 to 32 GB.

blocks.text: Find the real parts of this laptop. Change nothing.

items: Press **Ctrl + Shift + Esc** to open Task Manager, and choose **Performance**.
Click **CPU**, and note the processor's name, its cores and its logical processors.
Click **Memory**, and note the total RAM. Note also whether it says how many slots are used.
Click **Disk**, and note its type (SSD or HDD) and its capacity.
Click **GPU** if you see it, and note its name.
Now look at the outside of the laptop. List every port, and what each one is for.
Write this laptop's specification as a small table. Then say which part you'd upgrade first for your degree work, and why, if it were possible.

blocks.text: Keep this list, as you'll use it in your course project.

rubric: I wrote a specification from real readings on this laptop.
I identified every port on it.
I gave a reason for which part I'd upgrade first.

exercises.question: Your laptop works but is getting very hot and slowing down. Which part's job should you think about first?
exercises.answer: Cooling. Check that the vents aren't blocked. A processor slows itself down when it's too hot.

exercises.question: Which part keeps your files when the laptop is off, and which holds what you're using now?
exercises.answer: Storage keeps them with the power off. Memory (RAM) holds what's in use.

exercises.question: Why can't you normally replace the processor in a phone?
exercises.answer: It's usually a system on a chip, fixed to the board, combined with other parts.

summary: The motherboard connects the processor, memory, storage, graphics and everything else.
The processor works, memory holds what's in use, and storage keeps data with the power off.
Heat matters: a hot processor slows itself down.
A system on a chip combines parts and saves power, but it can't be upgraded.
Read a specification part by part. No single number decides how fast a computer is.

lessons.title: The layers of software
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.goal: Explain how software sits in layers between you and the hardware, tell apart firmware, the operating system, drivers and applications, and say why updates and licences matter.
lessons.why: When something breaks, the first useful question is which layer failed. It's the difference between reinstalling an app and replacing a part. The layers also explain security: an attacker who reaches a lower layer controls everything above it. And your later operating systems and security courses all build on this picture.

blocks.text: This short clip shows the operating system starting from storage, loading into memory, and letting programs use devices. The lesson adds firmware, licences and updates.
**Software** is instructions stored as bits. Most programs don't talk to hardware directly. They ask the layer beneath them, so that each layer only has to understand the one next to it.

blocks.code:
You
  Applications        Word, Chrome, a game
  Operating system    Windows, its services and tools
  Kernel and drivers  The core, and device-specific code
  Firmware            Built-in startup and device code
  Hardware            Processor, memory, storage

blocks.text: Worked example: pressing Save

items: In the **application**, you press Ctrl + S. The app asks the operating system to write a file.
The **operating system** checks that you're allowed to, and works out where it goes.
A **driver** turns that into commands that this particular drive understands.
The **firmware** inside the drive places the bits onto its storage.

blocks.text: The app doesn't need to know what brand of drive you have. So one app works on millions of different computers. This idea, hiding details behind a simple interface, is called **abstraction**, and you will see it everywhere in computing.

head: Layer
What it is
Examples
Where it's kept
rows: Low-level code built into a device
UEFI on the motherboard, code inside a drive or printer
Code that lets the operating system use one kind of device
Storage, loaded into memory when it starts
A small tool that maintains the system

blocks.text: **System software** means firmware, drivers, operating systems and utilities: software that runs the machine. **Application software** does things for the user.
An **operating system** does several jobs:

head: Job
What it means
rows: Starts them, and shares the processor among them
Gives each program its own space
Organises storage into files and folders
Uses drivers to talk to hardware
Windows, icons, or commands to type

blocks.text: Thinking "the app doesn't work" means the computer is broken. Test another app. If only one app fails, look at that app. If a device fails in every app, suspect its driver or hardware. If everything fails, look lower down.

blocks.question: A printer prints fine from one laptop, and not from yours. Which layer should you check first?
blocks.answer: The driver on your laptop, or the app's settings. The printer's hardware clearly works, because it prints from another laptop.

blocks.text: You reach an operating system through an interface. A **graphical user interface** (GUI) uses windows and icons. A **command-line interface** (CLI) uses typed commands. They reach the same system: opening a folder by clicking and by typing a command gets you to the same place. Servers often have no GUI at all, and that's why you'll learn the command line later.
An **application programming interface** (API) is how programs ask other software for something. When an app "asks the operating system to write a file", it's using an API.

head: Term
Meaning
Examples
rows: Owned by a company, and the code is usually private
The code is public, and you may study and change it under its licence
Free to use, but the code is usually private

blocks.text: Free in price isn't the same as open. When you "buy" software, you usually buy a **licence**, which is permission to use it under certain conditions, and you don't own the program.

Software has bugs, and some bugs are security holes. A **patch** or update fixes them. When a fix is published, attackers can study what was fixed, so devices that stay unpatched become easy targets. This is why updating is one of the most effective protections you have.

Update from the system's own update settings or the maker's official site. Never from a pop-up on a website saying your computer is infected or needs an update. That's a common way to deliver malware. And avoid "cracked" paid software, since it's often used to spread malware and it can't safely be updated. Free legal options exist for nearly everything in this course.

A program can normally only do what the layers below let it do. So malware that gets into a driver or the firmware can hide from everything above it, and it's much harder to detect and remove. That's why operating systems restrict who can install drivers, and why you should be cautious when something asks for administrator permission.
Look at the layers on this laptop, without changing or installing anything.

items: Press the Windows key, type `about`, and open **About your PC**. Note your Windows edition and version, which identify your operating system.

Press the Windows key, type `device manager`, and open it. Expand **Display adapters**. Double-click one, and look at the **Driver** tab. Note its provider and date. Then close it, and change nothing.
Press the Windows key, type `windows update`, and open it. Note the date of the last check. If updates are waiting and it's a good time, you may install them.
List three applications you use. For each, say whether it's proprietary or open source, and how you know.
Pick one real problem you've had on a computer. Say which layer you now think it was in, and why.

rubric: I found my real operating system version and one real driver.
I classified three of my own applications.
I placed a real problem in a layer, and gave a reason.

exercises.question: Classify each: a printer driver, Google Chrome, Windows, the code inside an SSD.
exercises.answer: System software (driver), application, system software (operating system), firmware.

exercises.question: You install a new graphics driver and the screen then flickers in every program. Which layer is the suspect?
exercises.answer: The driver, because the problem is in every application and it started just after the change. Roll it back.

exercises.question: "It's free, so it's open source." Is this correct?
exercises.answer: No. Free in price doesn't mean that the code is public or that you may change it. Check the licence.

summary: Software comes in layers: applications, operating system, kernel and drivers, firmware, then hardware.
Each layer hides details from the one above. This is abstraction.
A driver lets the operating system use one kind of device.
A licence is permission to use software. Free in price doesn't mean open source.
Update through official routes. Lower layers are more powerful, so they're more dangerous if compromised.

lessons.courses: UNIPORT (expected) COS 101, CSC 101, IFT 211 · NOUN COS101
lessons.goal: Convert whole numbers between binary and decimal by hand in both directions, work out how many values a number of bits can hold, and explain how the same bits can mean a number or a letter.
lessons.why: Binary questions appear in first-year computing exams, and the idea runs through everything afterwards. Bits explain why a file is the size it is, why your 500 GB drive shows less in Windows, how colours and text are stored, how IP addresses and subnet masks work, and why a program can overflow. In security and networking you will read bits for real, so this needs to be automatic and not just understood once.

sections.title: Place value, in the system you already know

blocks.text: The video teaches place value and binary counting up to 6. It stops part way through counting to 7, so this lesson finishes that and adds conversion, bytes and text.
You read 305 without thinking, but look at what it means. Each position has a value, and each position is worth ten times the one to its right.
Add the contributions and you get 305. This is base 10, or **decimal**. It has ten digits, 0 to 9, and the place values are powers of 10: 1, 10, 100, 1000.
Nothing about this needs ten. Humans probably chose it because of fingers. A computer's circuits work best with two clearly different states, on and off, so it uses two digits.
In base 2, or **binary**, the only digits are 0 and 1. A single binary digit is a **bit**. Each position is worth twice the one to its right.
Learn this row by heart, because you will use it for years. To read a binary number, write it under the place values and add those with a 1.
Worked example: binary to decimal
Try it first. Press the bits below to turn them on and off, and watch the total change.

spec.alt: Eight binary digits you can switch on and off, with place values 128 down to 1 and the decimal total shown beneath.

blocks.text: Now convert `101101` to decimal. It has six digits, so the places are 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Always line up from the right. The rightmost bit is always worth 1, however long the number is. Here is the count the video begins, carried further:

blocks.question: What is `1010` in decimal?

blocks.text: Use repeated subtraction. Find the largest place value that fits, write a 1 there, subtract, and carry on with what remains. Every place you skip gets a 0.

Convert 37.

Does it fit in what remains?
Bit
Remaining

blocks.text: Read the bits from top to bottom: **100101**. Now check by going back: 32 + 4 + 1 = 37. Always check, because it takes seconds and catches most slips.
Leaving out a 0 for a place you skipped. 37 is `100101`, not `1111`. Writing out all the place values first stops this happening.

Some textbooks, including course material you may be given, teach another way: divide by 2 repeatedly and read the remainders from bottom to top. It gives the same answer. For 37 the remainders are 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1 from first to last, and reading them backwards gives 100101. Use whichever your lecturer expects in an exam, and use the other to check.

Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so **n bits give 2^n different values**. With 3 bits there are 8 patterns, 000 to 111, which count from 0 to 7. The largest value is always one less than the number of patterns, because one pattern is used for 0.
Eight bits make a **byte**, the basic unit of size in computing.

head: Bits
Patterns
Unsigned range
Where you meet it
rows: One byte, each part of an IPv4 address

blocks.text: So when a later lesson shows an address like 192.168.1.10, you will know why no part is above 255. Each part is one byte.

**Unsigned** means every pattern counts as zero or above. Computers can also store negative numbers using an agreed pattern, called two's complement, which you will meet in a later course. A fixed number of bits can run out, too. In 8 unsigned bits, 255 is `11111111`, and adding 1 needs a ninth bit. If there is nowhere to put it, the value wraps to 0. This is **overflow**, and it has caused real software failures.
File sizes

A kilobyte is about a thousand bytes, a megabyte about a million, a gigabyte about a billion. Drive makers count in exact powers of 1000, while Windows measures in powers of 1024 and still writes GB. A "500 GB" drive holds 500,000,000,000 bytes. Divide by 1024 three times and you get about 465.7, so Windows reports roughly 465 GB. No space is missing. Two different units are sharing a name.

Network speeds are normally in bits, and file sizes in bytes. A 10 megabit per second line moves at most 1.25 megabytes per second, because you divide by 8. That is worth remembering when you plan a download on paid data.

sections.title: The same bits can mean different things

blocks.text: Bits have no meaning of their own. Meaning comes from how a program agrees to read them. The byte `01000001` is the number 65, and under the ASCII and Unicode text standards, 65 is also the capital letter A.

Colours work the same way. A screen colour is commonly three bytes, for red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255. Images, sound and programs are all just long runs of bits, read according to an agreed format.
This is why a file with the wrong extension opens as nonsense. The bits are fine, but the program is reading them under the wrong agreement.
You can check all of this in Python, which you will use soon:

print(2 ** 8)

lessons.goal: Convert between binary, hexadecimal and decimal by hand, explain why programmers use hexadecimal, and work out real file sizes and download times.
lessons.why: Long binary numbers are nearly impossible for a person to read. Hexadecimal is how you'll actually see bits: in colour codes, memory addresses, IPv6 addresses, hashes and security tools. It's on first-year exams, and you'll meet it for the rest of your career. Sizes are just as practical, because they tell you what a download will cost in data, and whether it fits.

blocks.text: David Malan introduces hexadecimal's 16 digits and how one hex digit stands for four bits, using colours as the example. Sizes and conversion practice come from this lesson.

Humans misread long strings of 0s and 1s. Is `1011011011100011` the same as `1011011011100111`? You had to look hard. Decimal would be shorter, but it doesn't line up neatly with bits. **Hexadecimal**, or **hex**, solves both problems.
Hex is base 16. It needs sixteen digits, so after 9 it borrows letters.
The key fact: **one hex digit is exactly four bits**, because 2^4 = 16. So a byte, which is 8 bits, is always exactly two hex digits. That's why hex is so convenient.
To show that a number is hex and not decimal, people write `0x` in front (`0x2F`), or `#` for colours. Otherwise `10` could mean ten or sixteen. Upper and lower case letters mean the same.
Binary to hex
Split into groups of four from the **right**, then replace each group.
If the leftmost group is short, add zeros on the left: `101101` becomes `0010 1101`, which is `0x2D`.
Hex to binary
Replace each hex digit with its four bits.
Hex to decimal
Place values are powers of 16: 1, 16, 256.
Decimal to hex
Divide by 16. The result is the left digit, and the remainder is the right digit, for numbers under 256.

blocks.text: Reading a letter as its own value. In `0x1A`, the A means 10, so it's 16 + 10 = 26. And `0x10` isn't ten. It's sixteen.

lessons.title: How letters become numbers
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.goal: Decode text from bytes using ASCII, explain why Unicode replaced it, work out how many bytes text takes in UTF-8, and recognise what goes wrong when encodings are mixed up.
lessons.why: All text in every program, email and database is stored as numbers. Knowing how explains garbled characters, why a file is the size it is, and why a tiny invisible difference can change a hash. In security, attackers abuse this: a web address can use a look-alike letter from another alphabet, so understanding encodings directly protects you.

blocks.text: David Malan shows that bits can stand for letters once everyone agrees on a mapping, then decodes bytes into the word HI using an ASCII chart. The details of Unicode and encoding problems come from this lesson.

A computer only stores bits, so to store a letter we must **agree** which number stands for it. That agreement is a **character encoding**. A **character** is one letter, digit, space or symbol. Nothing about the letter A says it should be 65. People simply decided, and everyone followed.
**ASCII** was published in the 1960s for American English. It uses 7 bits, so it has 128 possible values.

head: Range
What's there
rows: Invisible control characters, such as newline (10) and tab (9)

blocks.text: Some useful patterns are built in. Letters are in order, so B is 66 and C is 67. Each lower case letter is exactly 32 above its capital: A is 65, and a is 97.

Thinking the digit `7` has the value 7 when it's stored as text. The character `7` is stored as 55. That's why the text "12" and the number 12 are different in a program, and why you must convert between them.
Worked example: decoding bytes
Decode `01001000 01001001`, as the video does.
So it spells **HI**. The same bytes could mean the numbers 72 and 73 in another program. The bits don't change, only how they're read.

blocks.code:
print(ord("H"))
print(chr(73))
print(bin(ord("H")))
print("HI".encode("ascii"))
print(list("HI".encode("ascii")))

blocks.question: Using A = 65, what does the sequence 67, 65, 66 spell?

sections.title: The world needs more than 128 characters

blocks.text: ASCII has no room for `₦`, for Igbo letters like `ụ`, for Yoruba's `ẹ`, or for Arabic, Chinese or emoji. For years, different countries used different encodings, so the same bytes showed as different letters on different computers.

**Unicode** fixed this by giving every character in the world one number, called its **code point**, written like `U+20A6`. It covers well over 100,000 characters across the world's scripts, plus symbols and emoji. The first 128 are exactly the ASCII codes.
Unicode decides the numbers. An **encoding** decides how to store these numbers as bytes. The usual choice is **UTF-8**, which uses 1 to 4 bytes per character.
So old ASCII files are already valid UTF-8, and that's a big reason it won. It also means **characters and bytes aren't the same count**.

blocks.code:
for text in ["A", "é", "₦", "😀", "N500", "₦500"]:
    print(text, len(text), len(text.encode("utf-8")))

blocks.text: If a file is written in one encoding and read as another, the bytes get read wrongly. This garbled text is called **mojibake**.

blocks.code:
original = "₦500"
stored = original.encode("utf-8")
print(stored.decode("latin-1").encode("latin-1") == stored)
print(stored.decode("cp1252", errors="replace"))

blocks.text: If you see `â‚¦` on a page where you expected `₦`, you've met this. The bytes are fine, and the reader used the wrong agreement. The fix is to read it with the right encoding, not to edit the text.

Line endings differ too. Windows usually ends a line with two characters, carriage return and line feed (13, 10), and Linux with just one (10). Two files can look identical and still have different bytes, and so different hashes.
Because Unicode has so many characters, some look identical to others. The Cyrillic `а` (U+0430) looks exactly like the Latin `a` (U+0061).

blocks.code:
print("a" == "а")
print(ord("a"), ord("а"))

blocks.text: This allows **homograph attacks**, where a web address uses look-alike letters from another alphabet. Browsers try to show suspicious names in an encoded form starting `xn--`. If an address matters, type it yourself or use your own bookmark, rather than following a link.

lessons.goal: Explain how an image is stored as pixels and colour values, calculate an uncompressed image's size, tell bitmap from vector images, and say why zooming in can't add real detail.
lessons.why: Images make up much of what you store, send and pay data for. Knowing how they work lets you choose formats and sizes properly, and judge claims about "enhanced" photos. Later this feeds into digital forensics, where image metadata can reveal when and where a photo was taken, and into machine learning, where an image is just numbers to a program.

blocks.text: David Malan builds up from a black-and-white smiley made of single bits to full colour using red, green and blue bytes. This lesson adds calculations, formats and metadata.

A **bitmap image**, also called a **raster image**, is a rectangular grid of tiny dots called **pixels**. Each pixel has one colour, stored as bits. Look very closely at a screen, and you may see them.
The simplest image uses one bit per pixel: 1 for black, 0 for white, or the other way round.
If you squint, that's a smiley face. A file holding these bits, plus some information about its width and height, is a real image.
Screens make colours by mixing **red, green and blue** light, or **RGB**. Using one byte for each gives 256 levels of each colour, which is 24 bits per pixel.
Mixing light isn't like mixing paint: red and green light make yellow, and all three at full make white. And 24 bits gives 2^24, which is 16,777,216 possible colours.
**Bit depth** or **colour depth** is the number of bits per pixel. **Transparency** is often stored as a fourth byte, called the **alpha channel**.

blocks.question: What colour would red 255, green 0, blue 255 give?
blocks.answer: Magenta, a bright pinkish purple, from red and blue light with no green.

blocks.text: **Resolution** is the number of pixels across and down. A "1080p" image is 1920 x 1080 pixels.

blocks.code: uncompressed size in bytes = width x height x bytes per pixel

blocks.text: Worked example
A 1920 x 1080 image at 24 bits, which is 3 bytes, per pixel:

items: That's about 6.2 MB.

blocks.text: A 12-megapixel phone photo has 12 million pixels, and at 3 bytes each that's 36 MB uncompressed. Yet the file on your phone may be only a few MB. That's **compression**, the subject of a later lesson.

blocks.code:
def image_bytes(width, height, bytes_per_pixel=3):
    return width * height * bytes_per_pixel

print(image_bytes(1920, 1080))
print(image_bytes(4000, 3000) / 1_000_000)

blocks.text: Thinking that more megapixels always means a better photo. Sensor size, lens and light often matter more. A small file sent via a messaging app has usually been heavily compressed too, so it may have lost detail.

sections.title: You can't add detail that isn't there

blocks.text: Zoom in far enough and you see squares. The information between those pixels was never recorded. Films show detectives pressing "enhance" to read a number plate from a blurry photo, and the lecture even shows clips of this. Real software can only guess or sharpen what's there. Modern AI can make a blurry image look sharp, but it's **inventing** plausible detail, and that isn't evidence of what was actually there.
That matters a great deal in investigations: an AI-enhanced face can look convincing, and it may be wrong.
Not all images are grids.

head: Bitmap
Vector
rows: Shapes described by maths: "a circle here, this size"
SVG, and PDF can contain vectors

blocks.text: Image files hold more than pixels. **EXIF** metadata can include the camera, the date and time, and even the GPS location where a photo was taken.

A photo posted online may reveal where you live, if its location data stays in the file. Many large sites remove it, but not all do, and files sent as documents often keep it. Turn off location for your camera if you don't need it. For your faceless channel, this matters a lot: check your images before you post them.
In forensics, the same metadata is useful evidence, though it can be edited, so it isn't proof by itself.

lessons.title: How sound and video become numbers
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Multimedia
lessons.goal: Explain how sound is sampled and how video is built from frames, calculate raw sizes for both, and tell a container format from a codec.
lessons.why: Sound and video are what eat your data and your storage. These calculations tell you what a lecture download really costs before you start it. They also explain why a file sometimes won't play, and they're useful for your channel, where you'll choose formats and quality every week.

sections.title: Sound is a wave, measured many times a second

blocks.text: This segment explains video: flip-book frames, keyframes that save space, and containers that hold video and audio tracks together. Sound sampling is taught here in writing.

Sound is air pressure rising and falling as a wave. A microphone turns that into a changing electrical signal. To store it, a computer measures the signal many times a second. Each measurement is a **sample**, and each sample is stored as a number.

Higher values give better quality and larger files. People hear up to about 20,000 Hz at most, and a sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency you want to capture. That's why 44,100 Hz is enough for music, and why voice calls can sound fine with far less.

blocks.code: raw audio bytes per second = sample rate x (bit depth / 8) x channels

blocks.text: Worked example: one minute of CD audio

items: Per second: 44,100 x 2 bytes x 2 channels = 176,400 bytes.
Per minute: 176,400 x 60 = 10,584,000 bytes, about 10.6 MB.

blocks.code:
def audio_bytes(seconds, rate=44100, bits=16, channels=2):
    return seconds * rate * (bits // 8) * channels

print(audio_bytes(1))
print(audio_bytes(60))

blocks.text: An MP3 of that minute might be around 1 MB, thanks to compression.

blocks.question: A voice note is recorded at 8,000 Hz, 8 bits, in mono. How many bytes does each second take, raw?
blocks.answer: 8,000 x 1 x 1 = 8,000 bytes a second.

blocks.text: **MIDI** is different, and the lecture mentions it too. It stores instructions such as "play this note now", not the sound itself, so its files are tiny, and they can sound different on different devices.

sections.title: Video is a fast flip book

blocks.text: A video is a series of still images called **frames**, shown fast enough that your brain sees motion, just like a flip book. The speed is the **frame rate**, in frames per second (fps). Films are usually 24 fps, and much online video is 30.

blocks.code: raw video bytes per second = width x height x bytes per pixel x frames per second

blocks.text: Worked example: why video must be compressed
One second of 1920 x 1080 at 3 bytes per pixel and 30 fps:

items: One frame: 1920 x 1080 x 3 = 6,220,800 bytes.
One second: 6,220,800 x 30 = 186,624,000 bytes, about 187 MB.
One hour: about 672 GB.

blocks.text: A real one-hour film at that size is often about 1 to 4 GB, which is over a hundred times smaller.

Most frames look almost the same as the one before. So instead of storing every frame fully, video stores a complete **keyframe** now and then, and between them only what changed. In a lecture, the wall doesn't move, so very little changes.

This is why a person talking takes much less data than a football match, and why fast scenes can go blocky on a slow connection. Quality is often described by **bitrate**, the bits used per second of video. To estimate size:

blocks.code: size in bytes = bitrate in bits per second x seconds / 8

blocks.text: A 2 Mbps video for 10 minutes: 2,000,000 x 600 / 8 = 150,000,000 bytes, which is 150 MB.
These two are commonly confused.

lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Multimedia
lessons.goal: Explain lossless and lossy compression, run a simple compression method by hand and in code, and choose the right format for a real file.
lessons.why: Compression is why your phone can hold thousands of photos, and why a video can reach you over a mobile connection at all. Choosing the right format saves you data and storage, and stops you damaging important files. The idea of finding and removing patterns also connects to statistics and to how some security tools work.

sections.title: The idea: say it in fewer bits

blocks.text: David Malan uses a blue sky to show that a file needn't store the same colour over and over, then compares lossless formats with lossy JPEG, including a badly over-compressed sunflower. This lesson adds run-length coding by hand and the limits of compression.

**Compression** means storing the same information, or close to it, in fewer bits. It works because real data has patterns and repetition. Instead of "blue, blue, blue, blue, blue", you can store "5 blue".

head: Type
What it does
Can you get the exact original back?
Examples
rows: Also throws away detail you may not notice

blocks.text: The **compression ratio** compares sizes. A file that goes from 10 MB to 2 MB has a ratio of 5 to 1.
The simplest lossless method is **run-length encoding** (RLE). It replaces a run of the same value with a count and the value.
Worked example

blocks.code:
Original:   BBBBBBWWWBBBBB    14 characters
Encoded:    6B3W5B             6 characters
Decoded:    BBBBBB WWW BBBBB  exactly the original

blocks.text: Decoding gives back exactly what you started with, so it's lossless. It's excellent for simple graphics with big flat areas. But watch what happens with varied data:

blocks.code:
Original:   BWBWBW   6 characters
Encoded:    1B1W1B1W1B1W   12 characters

blocks.text: It got **bigger**. No compression method can shrink everything, because there aren't enough shorter outputs to give every possible file a different one.

blocks.code:
def rle(text):
    out = ""
    i = 0
    while i < len(text):
        run = 1
        while i + run < len(text) and text[i + run] == text[i]:
            run = run + 1
        out = out + str(run) + text[i]
        i = i + run
    return out

print(rle("BBBBBBWWWBBBBB"))
print(rle("BWBWBW"))

blocks.question: Encode `AAAABBC` using run-length encoding. Is it shorter?
blocks.answer: `4A2B1C`, which is 6 characters instead of 7. It's only slightly shorter, because the runs are short.

blocks.text: A lossy format decides what you won't miss. A JPEG keeps brightness detail more carefully than colour detail, because human eyes notice brightness more. An MP3 removes sounds that louder sounds would hide from your ear. At mild settings, you can hardly tell. Push it too far, and you get blocky patches in pictures and watery-sounding audio, which are known as **artifacts**.
Each lossy save loses more

Repeatedly editing and saving a JPEG. Each save throws away a little more. Compressing an already compressed image makes it worse, and it can't bring back what's gone. Keep an original, and export a copy.

blocks.text: JPEG on text or diagrams leaves smudges around the edges. PNG on a photo gives a very large file. So match the format to the content.
GIF can hold several images, which is why it's used for short loops, like the cat in the lecture. Its limit of 256 colours comes from using 8 bits per pixel.

blocks.text: A ZIP file compresses and packs together other files, losslessly.

head: Compresses well
Hardly compresses

blocks.text: Zipping a video won't save you noticeable data, because it's already been compressed.
Encrypted data also doesn't compress, because good encryption makes data look random, with no patterns to remove. So compress first, then encrypt.
Here's the same principle measured with Python, comparing repetitive text with random bytes:

blocks.code:
import random
import zlib

print(len(zlib.compress(random_bytes)) > 9900)

blocks.text: Ten thousand repeated letters shrink to under 100 bytes, while ten thousand random bytes hardly shrink at all.

Attackers often hide malware inside ZIP files, including ones with passwords, partly because some scanners can't look inside them. Don't open an unexpected ZIP from a message, even if the password comes with it. A **zip bomb** is a tiny archive that expands to enormous size, to crash the tools that open it.

lessons.source: OpenStax · Introduction to Computer Science
lessons.goal: Explain how transistors become logic gates, work out truth tables for AND, OR, NOT, XOR and NAND, and trace how gates add two binary digits.
lessons.why: This is where bits become thinking. Every calculation a computer makes comes down to these few simple gates, and that's a wonderful thing to understand. Digital logic is a full course in your degree path, and the same AND, OR and NOT come back in programming, in sets and in search queries. It also explains how a computer can possibly add numbers at all.

blocks.text: This lesson has no lecture, because I didn't find a free segment that fits well enough and whose transcript I've checked. The writing covers it fully. Nand2Tetris, listed below, is an excellent free course if you want to go much further.

A bit needs something physical to hold it. A **transistor** is a tiny electronic switch with no moving parts: a small signal on one connection controls whether current flows through the other two. On means 1 and off means 0.
A modern processor holds billions of them on a chip about the size of a fingernail. One transistor does almost nothing, but connected in the right patterns they can make decisions.
A **logic gate** takes one or more input bits, and produces an output bit by a fixed rule. A **truth table** lists the output for every possible input. With two inputs there are always four rows.
NOT
NOT flips its one input.
AND
AND gives 1 only if **both** inputs are 1. Think: a door that needs two keys.
OR
OR gives 1 if **at least one** input is 1. Think: a room light with two switches, either of which turns it on.
In everyday speech "or" often means one or the other but not both. In logic, OR includes both. The gate for "one but not both" is XOR.
XOR and NAND
**XOR** (exclusive or) gives 1 only if the inputs **differ**. **NAND** is NOT AND: it gives 0 only if both inputs are 1.

NAND has a remarkable property: **every other gate can be built from NAND gates alone**. So in principle a whole computer can be built from one type of gate, and this is what the Nand2Tetris course does.

blocks.question: What's the output of (1 AND 0) OR (NOT 0)?
blocks.answer: 1 AND 0 is 0. NOT 0 is 1. 0 OR 1 is 1.

blocks.text: The output of one gate can feed another. To work out a circuit, go step by step and add a column for each stage. For X = (A AND B) OR (NOT A):
With n inputs a truth table needs 2^n rows, the same doubling as in binary.
Python's `&`, `|` and `^` work on bits, so you can check any of these:

blocks.output:
0 0 AND 0 OR 0 XOR 0
0 1 AND 0 OR 1 XOR 1
1 0 AND 0 OR 1 XOR 1
1 1 AND 1 OR 1 XOR 0

blocks.text: Here's the moment it all comes together. Add two single bits by hand:
Look at the Sum column: it matches XOR. Look at the Carry column: it matches AND. So one XOR gate and one AND gate add two bits. This circuit is called a **half adder**.

To add longer numbers, you also need to handle the carry coming in from the column to the right. A **full adder** takes three inputs, and chaining 64 of them adds two 64-bit numbers. That's inside the processor's **arithmetic logic unit**.
Worked example: full adder step
Add A = 1, B = 1, with a carry in of 1.

items: A XOR B = 0.
That XOR carry-in = 0 XOR 1 = **1**, which is the sum.
Carry out: (A AND B) OR (carry-in AND (A XOR B)) = 1 OR 0 = **1**.

blocks.text: 1 + 1 + 1 is 3, which is binary 11: sum 1, carry 1. It works.

rows: Search filters, such as `site:` plus a word
Encryption: a bit XOR a key bit, and XOR again gets it back

blocks.text: XOR's reversibility is at the heart of many ciphers. You'll meet it again in cryptography.
Gates that hold a value, rather than only computing one, can be built too, by feeding outputs back into inputs. That's how memory cells work, which you'll study in Computer Organisation.

lessons.title: How a processor runs a program
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.goal: Name the parts of a processor, trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle through a small program by hand, and explain what clock speed and cores really do.
lessons.why: This is what "running a program" actually means. Once you can trace it, programming stops being mysterious, and so do many security bugs, which trick a processor into treating data as instructions. It's core exam material in computer architecture, and it tells you what a processor's specification really promises.

blocks.text: David Malan shows what a CPU physically is, then explains cores, hyperthreading and systems on a chip. It doesn't cover the fetch-decode-execute cycle, which this lesson teaches.
A **processor** or **CPU** carries out instructions one small step at a time. Its main parts are:

head: Part
Job
rows: Directs everything, deciding what happens next
Does arithmetic and comparisons, using the gates from the last lesson
A few tiny, very fast storage slots inside the processor
A special register holding the address of the next instruction
A steady pulse that keeps everything in step

blocks.text: **Memory** is like a long row of numbered boxes. Each box's number is its **address**. Both the program's instructions and its data sit in memory. This design, keeping instructions and data in the same memory, is called the **stored-program** or **von Neumann** model.
A processor repeats one loop, billions of times a second.

items: **Fetch:** read the instruction at the address in the program counter, and add 1 to the program counter.
**Decode:** work out what that instruction means.
**Execute:** do it, which may use the ALU or memory.

blocks.text: Then it goes again. That's it. Everything your laptop does is this loop, repeated.

Instructions are extremely simple. A real processor's instructions are of this kind: load a number from memory into a register, add two registers, store a register into memory, or jump to another address.
Worked example: tracing a tiny program
Here's a made-up machine with one working register, called A. The program adds the values at addresses 10 and 11, and stores the result at address 12.
Trace it, one cycle at a time.

blocks.question: If memory 10 held 20 and memory 11 held 3, what would memory 12 hold at the end?
blocks.answer: 23. The same instructions run on different data.

blocks.text: Decisions and loops

A **jump** instruction sets the program counter to another address. A **conditional jump** does so only if something is true, such as a register being zero. Every `if` and every loop in any programming language becomes this in the end.
Instructions are stored as bits, like everything else. The processor treats the bits at the program counter as an instruction, whatever they really are.

This is the root of many serious attacks. If an attacker can get their own data into memory and make the processor jump to it, the data is run as instructions. This is the idea behind many **memory corruption** attacks, such as buffer overflows. Modern systems defend against this by marking memory as data-only, and you'll study this in security courses.

The **clock speed** is the number of pulses per second. 3 GHz means 3 billion cycles a second. Instructions may take several cycles, or modern designs may finish several per cycle, so cycles aren't quite the same as instructions.

head: Claim
Reality
rows: No. Design matters, so compare within a similar generation
It speeds up when busy (turbo) and slows when idle or hot

blocks.text: A clip in a later lesson says a gigahertz means a billion "things" per second. That's a good first idea, and the truth is the rule above.

A **core** is a complete processing unit: its own control unit, ALU and registers. Two cores can truly run two things at the same moment. **Hyperthreading** lets one core keep two threads ready, so it looks like two **logical processors** to Windows, although it isn't as fast as two full cores.
A program only gains from many cores if it was written to split its work. So 8 cores won't help a program that only uses one, and this is why a higher core count doesn't always feel faster.
Thinking that 2 cores make everything twice as fast. Many tasks can't be split evenly, and the parts that must run in order limit the gain.

Each processor family understands its own **instruction set**. Most Windows laptops use **x86-64**, and most phones use **ARM**. A program compiled for one won't run directly on the other. That's why software downloads often ask about your system type, and the next lesson explains how programs get turned into these instructions.

It loops: fetch, decode, execute, billions of times a second.
Instructions and data both sit in memory, as bits.
Conditional jumps are what every `if` and loop become.

lessons.title: From code you write to code the machine runs
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Programming
lessons.goal: Explain the levels of programming language, tell compiling from interpreting, follow how source code becomes machine code, and say why a program runs on one system but not another.
lessons.why: You'll write Python, C, SQL and more during your studies. Knowing what happens to your code makes error messages make sense, and explains why some languages are faster than others. It also matters for security: running a program you can't read means trusting it, and reverse engineering in your final year is this process run backward.

blocks.text: David Malan asks how human-readable code can run on a machine that only understands 0s and 1s, then explains compilers and interpreters. Language levels and assembly are added in this lesson.

The last lesson showed that a processor only understands machine instructions, as bits. People can't comfortably write in bits. So we write in languages closer to human thinking, and let a program translate them. The text you write is called **source code**.

head: Level
Example
What it's like
rows: Short names, one for each machine instruction
Close to human thinking. One line can become many instructions

blocks.text: Machine code and assembly are **low-level**, because they're tied to one processor family. High-level languages such as Python, C and Java can usually be used on many kinds of computers.
Worked example: one line, many steps
The Python line `total = price * quantity` could become steps like these.

blocks.code:
LOAD   price into a register
LOAD   quantity into another register
MULTIPLY the two registers
STORE  the result into total

blocks.text: That's the same style of instructions you traced by hand in the last lesson.

A **compiler** translates all of your source code into machine code **before** the program runs. The result is a separate file, on Windows usually a `.exe`. You can give that file to someone who doesn't have your source code or the compiler.

blocks.code: hello.c  -->  compiler  -->  hello.exe  -->  runs on the processor

blocks.text: C, C++, Rust and Go are usually compiled. If the source has a grammar mistake, the compiler refuses to produce anything, and tells you. You get a **syntax error**. The steps of a full build include checking the code, translating it, and joining it with other code it needs, called **linking**.
An **interpreter** reads your source code and carries it out as the program runs. You need the interpreter on the machine, and you keep the source code.

blocks.code: hello.py  -->  interpreter  -->  actions happen as it goes

head: Compiled
Interpreted
rows: Source code, and the person needs the interpreter
May appear only when that line is reached

blocks.text: Real life is less tidy. Python first compiles your code to an in-between form called **bytecode**, and the Python interpreter runs that. Java does something similar. Many browsers compile JavaScript as it runs. So "compiled" or "interpreted" describes how a language is usually run, more than the language itself.
You can actually look at Python's bytecode:

blocks.code:
import dis
def total(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity
names = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(total)]
print("BINARY_OP" in names)
print("RETURN_VALUE" in names)

blocks.text: Those names are bytecode instructions, which the Python interpreter steps through much as a processor steps through machine code.

blocks.question: You send a friend `report.py`, and they've never installed Python. What happens when they try to run it?
blocks.answer: It won't run as a program, because they need the interpreter. A compiled `.exe` for Windows wouldn't need it.

head: Kind
When
Example
rows: It runs, and gives the wrong answer

blocks.text: Believing a program without errors is correct. Logic errors give no message at all. Only testing against what you expected can find them, and that's why you predict before running.

A compiled program depends on two things: the **processor's instruction set**, as last lesson explained, and the **operating system**, which it asks for files, memory and more. So a Windows `.exe` built for x86-64 won't run directly on an Android phone, as both differ. An interpreted program can run on any system that has its interpreter, which is a big reason Python is so portable.
You can read source code. You can't easily read a compiled program. **Decompiling** and **reverse engineering** try to work backward, but names and comments are gone, so it's slow, skilled work.

Running a program means trusting it, with all your rights. Open source lets people inspect the code, but that doesn't guarantee that anyone did, or that the file you downloaded was built from that code. Get programs from official sources, and check the digest when one's offered, as you'll learn in the file integrity lesson. Reverse engineering is legal only within the limits of the law and any licence, so only do it on software you're allowed to examine, in a lab.

items: Press the Windows key, type `cmd`, and press Enter. Type `where python` and press Enter. Note whether Windows found an interpreter on this laptop. A path ending `WindowsApps\python.exe` is usually only a shortcut to the Microsoft Store. It's fine if Python isn't installed, as this app has its own.
In File Explorer, find a program file (`.exe`) in `C:\Windows`, such as `notepad.exe`. Note its size. Don't run or change anything. You can't read this file as text, because it's machine code.
In the editor, create all three kinds of error in turn: a syntax error, a runtime error, and a logic error in the function. Run each, and record what you saw. Which one gave no message?
Fix the function, and press **Test my code**.

exercises.question: Which is lowest level: Python, assembly or machine code?
exercises.answer: Machine code. Assembly is one step above it, and Python is high level.

exercises.question: A program runs, but it always reports totals that are too small. What kind of error is this?
exercises.answer: A logic error. It runs without a message, and gives the wrong answer.

exercises.question: Why might a C program run faster than the same program in Python?
exercises.answer: C is translated to machine code ahead of time. Python's bytecode is stepped through by an interpreter, which adds work.

exercises.question: You see `SyntaxError` before any of your Python lines have printed. Why did nothing run?
exercises.answer: Python compiles the file to bytecode first, and the grammar error stops it before it starts.

summary: Machine code is what runs. Assembly names its instructions. High-level languages are for people.
A compiler translates before running, and produces a separate program.
An interpreter carries out code while it runs. Python uses bytecode in between.
Syntax errors stop translation, runtime errors crash, and logic errors stay silent.
A compiled program depends on its processor type and operating system.

lessons.title: Memory and persistent storage
lessons.source: Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
lessons.courses: UNIPORT (expected) COS 101, CSC 101 · NOUN COS101, GST103
lessons.goal: Explain what the processor, RAM and storage each do, follow a document from opening to saving, and use Task Manager to tell which resource is really running short.
lessons.why: This explains everyday problems you can fix yourself: why unsaved work vanishes in a power cut, and why deleting files does not make a slow laptop faster. It also comes up in first-year exams, and it is the base for operating systems at 300 level. In security, what sits in memory and what stays on the drive decides what a forensic investigator can recover.

blocks.text: The video starts mid-sentence, on RAM, then spends some time on processor speed and cores. It ends as it introduces hard disks, so it never reaches SSDs. This lesson covers the rest, and it matters more than the clip for the check.

head: Part
Job
Speed
Keeps data without power?
rows: Working memory for what is running now
Keeps files and programs for later

blocks.text: **The processor** does the work: arithmetic, comparisons, deciding which instruction comes next. Its speed is given in gigahertz, where 1 GHz means a billion cycles a second. A **core** is an independent processing unit inside the chip, so a four-core processor can truly do four things at once. Clock speed alone does not decide how fast a computer feels, because the chip design and the amount of memory matter too.
**RAM**, or random access memory, is where programs and their data sit while in use. It is **volatile**: its contents depend on power, and when power goes, they go.

**Storage** is **non-volatile**, so it keeps its contents with the power off. A hard disk drive stores data on spinning magnetic platters with a moving arm. A solid-state drive, or SSD, stores it in flash memory chips with no moving parts, which is why it is so much faster and survives being knocked better.
"Memory" and "storage" are often mixed up in shops and adverts. "A laptop with 512 GB of memory" nearly always means storage. In this course and in exams, memory means RAM.

If RAM is so fast, why not use only RAM? Because it costs far more per gigabyte and forgets everything without power. And if storage keeps data, why not use only storage? Because it is far too slow for the processor to work from directly. The gap is huge: by rough, commonly quoted figures, reading from RAM takes around 100 nanoseconds, from an SSD around 100 microseconds, and from a hard disk around 10 milliseconds. So an SSD can be about a thousand times slower than RAM, and a hard disk about a hundred thousand times.

This is called the **memory hierarchy**: small and fast near the processor, large and slow further away. Inside the processor there are even smaller, faster stores called registers and cache. The computer constantly copies what it needs into the faster levels.
Here is what happens when you work on an assignment.

items: **Open.** The app reads the file from storage and copies it into RAM. The copy on the drive is untouched.
**Edit.** Your typing changes the copy in RAM. The processor does the work. The file on the drive is still the old version.
**Save.** The app writes the current version from RAM back to storage. Only now does the file on the drive change.
**Close or shut down.** RAM is released. The saved file remains.

blocks.text: So in a power cut, you lose everything since your last save, because only RAM held it. A laptop battery protects you from that for a while, and a desktop on mains power gets no such protection, unless it has a backup power unit.

Thinking autosave means your work is always safe. Autosave protects you only if it has actually written your changes to storage, and it runs at intervals or only under certain conditions. For Word, it may depend on the settings and on whether the file is in OneDrive. Press Ctrl + S yourself, and do it often.

blocks.question: You open a document, delete half of it and have not saved. The power fails. What is in the file on the drive?
blocks.answer: The full old version. Your deletion only happened to the copy in RAM, so losing power loses the deletion. This can actually rescue you.

blocks.text: Slow computers and full computers are different problems.

head: You see
Likely resource
What helps
What doesn't
rows: Everything slows when many apps or tabs are open
Close apps and tabs, or add RAM
Windows warns that the disk is full, or a download fails for lack of space
A single heavy task is slow while memory is fine
Wait, or use fewer heavy apps at once

blocks.text: When RAM runs out, Windows moves some of what is in memory to a **page file** on the drive. This keeps programs running but is far slower, so the whole machine drags, with the disk very busy. That is why low memory can show up as high disk activity.
Reading Task Manager
Press **Ctrl + Shift + Esc**, and choose **Performance**.

items: **Memory** shows how much RAM the machine has in total, and how much is in use right now.
**Disk** shows how busy each drive is as **Active time**, not how full it is. To see how full a drive is, right-click it in File Explorer and open Properties.
**CPU** shows how busy the processor is, and its speed and number of cores.

blocks.text: Live usage readings change second by second. Capacity, such as the total RAM, stays the same. Do not mix them up.

Windows 11's Notepad can bring back unsaved tabs, because it writes its session to disk in the background. That is a feature of that one app. Most programs will not save you this way, so do not rely on it.

Because RAM holds what programs are using right now, it can hold things that are never written to a file in plain form, such as an open document or a password you have just typed. That is why forensic investigators may try to capture memory before powering a machine down, since turning it off destroys that evidence. And data on a drive stays until overwritten, so a deleted file may be recoverable. Encrypting a drive is what protects you if the laptop is stolen. You will study this properly in digital forensics at NOUN.
Investigate this laptop, using real readings.

items: Open Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc and choose Performance.
Under Memory, write the total RAM and the amount in use. Under CPU, write the number of cores.
Open three apps you normally use, wait ten seconds and read Memory again. Close them, wait and read it again.
Open File Explorer, right-click drive C and choose Properties. Write the drive's capacity and free space.
Write which of these numbers are capacities and which are live readings. Based on what you found, which is the tighter resource on this laptop right now, and what would you do about it?

rubric: I took real readings from this laptop, before and after opening apps.
I told capacities apart from live usage readings.

exercises.question: Your laptop has plenty of free drive space, but it slows badly with 40 browser tabs open. Will deleting old videos help?
exercises.answer: No. That frees storage, while this looks like a RAM shortage. Closing tabs will help.

exercises.question: A friend says their computer has "16 GB of memory and 512 GB of memory". What do they most likely mean?
exercises.answer: 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage.

exercises.question: Why does restarting a computer often fix a slow machine, without deleting any files?
exercises.answer: It empties RAM and stops whatever was running, so memory and processor become free again. Storage is unchanged.

summary: The processor carries out instructions, RAM holds what is running now, and storage keeps data for later.
RAM is volatile and loses everything without power. Storage is non-volatile.
Opening copies a file into RAM, editing changes that copy, and only saving changes the drive.
Low RAM and a full drive are different problems with different fixes.
Disk Active time means how busy a drive is, not how full it is.
