lessons.title: How drives keep your data
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.goal: Explain how hard disks and SSDs physically store bits, compare them, say what deleting really does, and set up a backup that would survive a failure.
lessons.why: Every drive eventually fails, and when yours does, your preparation decides whether you lose four years of work or nothing. How drives store data also explains why deleted files can often be recovered, which is the basis of digital forensics, and why you should wipe a laptop properly before selling it.

blocks.text: David Malan shows a real hard disk, an animation of how bits are written magnetically, then solid-state and hybrid drives. Deleting and backups come from this lesson.
RAM forgets without power, so computers need **non-volatile storage**. There are two main kinds today.
Hard disk drives
A **hard disk drive** (HDD) stores bits on spinning metal or glass **platters** coated with a magnetic material. An **arm** with a tiny **read/write head** floats just above the surface.

items: **To write:** the head magnetises a tiny region one way or the other, standing for 0 or 1.
**To read:** the head senses which way each region is magnetised.

blocks.text: Platters spin thousands of times a minute, and 5,400 or 7,200 revolutions per minute (rpm) are common speeds. To reach data, the arm must move to the right ring, and then wait for the disk to spin round. This physical movement is why hard disks are so slow compared with chips, and why a drop while running can destroy one.
Solid-state drives

A **solid-state drive** (SSD) stores bits as electric charge in **flash memory** chips. With no moving parts, it reads any location almost instantly, and survives knocks far better. A USB flash drive and a phone's storage use similar technology.

Flash cells wear out, as the video says: each cell survives only a limited number of writes. Drives spread writes evenly to last longer, which is called **wear levelling**. For ordinary use, a good SSD lasts many years, but an SSD can fail suddenly and without warning.
The clip also mentions hybrid drives, which combine both. They are less common now that SSDs have got cheaper.

blocks.question: You're buying an external drive just to keep backups cheaply. Which type suits you better, and what's the risk?
blocks.answer: A hard disk is usually cheaper per GB. It's fragile, so handle it carefully and don't move it while it's running.

sections.title: How data is organised on a drive

blocks.text: A drive stores data in fixed-size blocks, called **sectors**, usually 512 or 4,096 bytes. A file larger than that takes many blocks, and they may not even be next to each other. The filesystem keeps track of which blocks belong to which file. You'll meet paths and folders in the next unit, and look deeper at this in the permissions lesson.
This surprises most people. When you delete a file:

items: **Recycle Bin:** it's just moved. Nothing is removed.
**Emptying the bin:** the filesystem marks the file's blocks as free to reuse. The bits themselves usually stay on the drive for now.
**Later:** new files may overwrite these blocks.

blocks.text: Think of removing a chapter from a book's contents page, without tearing out the pages. Until someone reuses those pages, the words are still there. That's why forensic tools and recovery software can often bring back deleted files, particularly on hard disks.

SSDs complicate this. A command called **TRIM** tells an SSD which blocks are free, and the drive may erase them soon after. So recovery from an SSD is often much harder, and it's not something you can rely on.

Believing that deleting or formatting wipes your data. A quick format mainly rewrites the filesystem's records. Before you sell or give away a laptop, use Windows' **Reset this PC** with its option to clean the drive, or rely on drive encryption from the beginning. Encrypted data is unreadable without the key, so it's safe even if deleted blocks remain.
Drives fail, laptops get stolen, and ransomware locks files. A popular rule is **3-2-1**:

head: Number
Meaning
Example
rows: So that one fault can't get them all
The laptop's SSD and an external drive
So that fire or theft can't take them all
A cloud copy, or a drive kept elsewhere

blocks.text: Two rules matter more than any product.

items: **Test restoring.** A backup you've never restored is only a hope. Bring one file back, and open it.
**Disconnect it.** Ransomware can encrypt a drive that's plugged in. Unplug your backup drive between uses.

blocks.text: Syncing isn't quite the same as backing up. If you delete or damage a file in a synced folder, the change can copy across too. Version history helps, so check whether your service keeps it, and for how long.
Cloud storage needs a strong password and two-factor sign-in, and costs data. And with your 4YOS records, make a backup from Settings on your own schedule.

Some warning signs that a hard disk is failing are clicking sounds, freezing, and very slow file access. If you see these, copy your most important files off at once, and don't run heavy repair tools first. An SSD may give no warning, and that's why you back up before anything goes wrong.
Work out where your real risks are, without moving or deleting anything you can't get back.

items: Press **Windows key + E**, right-click drive C, and open **Properties**. Note its capacity and free space. Open Task Manager's **Performance** tab, click **Disk**, and note whether it's an SSD or HDD.
List your three most important folders. For each, write how many copies exist, on how many types of storage, and whether one is elsewhere.
Pick your most important unbacked-up folder, and copy it to a second place now: an external drive, a flash drive or a cloud service you trust.
Test it: open one file from the copy, to confirm that it works.
Write what still needs doing to reach 3-2-1, and by what date.
Make a 4YOS backup from Settings, if you haven't.

rubric: I found the real type and capacity of my drive.
I made a real second copy of something important, and opened a file from it.
I wrote down what's still missing, with a date.

exercises.question: A friend deleted their file and emptied the bin an hour ago. Which is more likely to allow recovery, a hard disk or an SSD with TRIM, and what should they do at once?
exercises.answer: A hard disk. They should stop using the drive, because new writes can overwrite those blocks.

exercises.question: Your laptop and your backup drive are both in one bag that gets stolen. Which part of 3-2-1 did you miss?
exercises.answer: The 1: a copy somewhere else.

exercises.question: Why can't you trust a backup you've never restored?
exercises.answer: It may be incomplete, corrupted or missing key files. Only a real restore proves that it works.

summary: Hard disks store bits magnetically on spinning platters. SSDs store them as charge in chips.
SSDs are faster and tougher, and hard disks are cheaper per GB.
Deleting usually only marks space as free, so data often remains until overwritten.
To dispose of a laptop, use a proper reset with cleaning, or rely on encryption.
Follow 3-2-1. Test your restores, and keep backups disconnected.

lessons.pack: How Computers Work · Inside the machine
lessons.title: Why computers keep copies close by
lessons.source: David J. Malan · Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Hardware
lessons.goal: Order the levels of memory by speed and size, explain what a cache is and why it works, and calculate how much a cache speeds things up.
lessons.why: Caching is one of the most important ideas in all of computing. It explains why a laptop feels faster on the second try, why a page loads quicker when you return to it, and how the internet copes with billions of people. As a programmer, it will explain why two programs doing the same work can differ hugely in speed. And caches can leak information, which matters in security.

blocks.text: David Malan pictures memory as a funnel from disk down to the CPU, then uses a candy store's nearby stock to explain a cache. He also reads real cache sizes from Task Manager.
Fast memory is expensive, and cheap memory is slow. So computers use a little very fast memory and a lot of slow memory, arranged in levels. This is the **memory hierarchy**.

head: Level
Rough size
Rough access time
Survives power off?
rows: Hundreds of KB to a few MB

blocks.text: Those times are rough, commonly quoted figures, and they vary by machine. But the pattern is what matters. A nanosecond is a billionth of a second, and a microsecond is 1,000 nanoseconds. A millisecond is a million nanoseconds. So if an L1 access took 1 second, a hard disk access would take about 4 months.

blocks.code:
l1 = 1
disk = 10_000_000
print(disk / l1)
print(round(disk / 60 / 60 / 24, 1))

blocks.text: A **cache** is a small, fast store holding copies of things that were recently used or are likely to be needed soon. The word is pronounced like "cash".

In the video's example, a shop keeps a little stock right on the counter, so that it needn't walk to the store room for each customer. Note that the store room still has the real stock. A cache holds **copies**.

items: A **cache hit** means that what you wanted was in the cache. It's fast.
A **cache miss** means it wasn't. You fetch it from the slower level, usually keeping a copy for next time.

blocks.text: When a cache is full, something must be removed. A common rule is to throw out what was **least recently used**.
A small cache helps because programs don't use memory at random. They show **locality**:

head: Kind
Meaning
Example
rows: Something used now will probably be used again soon
Things near what you used will probably be used soon
The next item in a list

blocks.text: So caches fetch nearby data too, in chunks. A program that goes through a list in order runs much faster than one that jumps around memory, even though both do the same arithmetic.
Worked example: how much does it help?
Say a cache takes 1 ns, RAM takes 100 ns, and 95% of accesses are hits.

blocks.code:
average time = hit rate x cache time + miss rate x miss time
             = 0.95 x 1 + 0.05 x 100
             = 0.95 + 5
             = 5.95 ns

blocks.text: Without the cache, each access takes 100 ns. So a small cache makes access about 17 times faster on average. Notice too that the 5% of misses take up most of the time. Improving a hit rate from 95% to 99% gives 0.99 + 1 = 1.99 ns, about three times faster again.

blocks.question: With a hit rate of 90%, a 2 ns cache and 100 ns memory, what's the average access time?

blocks.text: Thinking that a cache is where your data is kept. It's a copy for speed. Clearing a cache doesn't delete the original, though things may be slower until the cache fills again.
This same idea appears at every level of computing.

head: Cache
Copy of
Saves
rows: Recently used parts of the drive
Popular videos, kept in nearby cities

blocks.text: This is why a program opens faster the second time, and why a site you've visited loads more quickly. It's also why Windows may seem to use a lot of memory when idle: unused RAM is put to work as a cache, and is released when programs need it.
Stale data

A cache's great problem is the copy going out of date, which is called being **stale**. If a site's page changes and your browser still shows the old one, reloading with **Ctrl + F5** usually fetches it fresh. Deciding when a copy is out of date is famously hard.

Caches keep traces of what you did. A browser cache and history may reveal sites you've visited, which is why you use a private window on a shared computer, and sign out. Investigators look in these places too. In deeper security work, attackers can sometimes learn secrets by timing whether something was in a processor cache, and those are called **side-channel attacks**.

items: Open Task Manager with **Ctrl + Shift + Esc**, go to **Performance**, then **CPU**, and note the L1, L2 and L3 cache sizes shown for this laptop. Then click **Memory**, and note the amount shown as cached.

Time it yourself: close a large program completely, then open it and count the seconds until it's ready. Close it, and open it again straight away. Compare the two, and explain the difference. Your result may vary with what else is running.
Open a website with lots of pictures, and note how long it takes. Close the tab, then open it again. Which cache helped?
Complete the functions in the editor, and press **Test my code**.
Use your function to find the hit rate that gives an average of under 5 ns, when the cache takes 1 ns and a miss takes 100 ns.

rubric: I read real cache sizes from this laptop.
I timed a real program opening twice, and explained the result.
My code passes the tests.
practice.starter:
def average_time(hit_rate, cache_time, miss_time):
    # hit rate x cache time + (1 - hit rate) x miss time
    return 0

def run_cache(requests, size):
    # Simulate a cache that holds "size" items. Throw out the oldest used item when full.
    # Return the number of hits.
    # The cache is a list, with the oldest used item at the front.
    cache = []
    hits = 0
    for item in requests:
        if item in cache:
            # A hit. Change the next line, so that hits goes up by 1
            hits = hits
            cache.remove(item)
            cache.append(item)
        else:
            # A miss: add the item at the end
            cache.append(item)
            # Too full? Remove the oldest. Finish this: if len(cache) > size: cache.pop(0)
    return hits

print(average_time(0.95, 1, 100))
print(run_cache(["a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "b"], 2))

lessons.tests:
assert round(average_time(0.95, 1, 100), 2) == 5.95, "95% hits, 1 ns and 100 ns gives 5.95"
assert average_time(1, 1, 100) == 1, "all hits gives just the cache time"
assert average_time(0, 1, 100) == 100, "no hits gives just the miss time"
assert run_cache([], 2) == 0, "no requests means no hits"
assert run_cache(["a", "a", "a"], 1) == 2, "the first a misses, and the next two hit"
assert run_cache(["a", "b", "c", "a"], 2) == 0, "a is thrown out before it is asked for again"
assert run_cache(["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"], 2) == 2, "using a keeps it in the cache"

exercises.question: Put in order, fastest first: RAM, SSD, L1 cache, register, hard disk.
exercises.answer: Register, L1 cache, RAM, SSD, hard disk.

exercises.question: A website loads faster the second time you visit it. Name the likely reason.
exercises.answer: Your browser cache kept copies of its files, so they weren't downloaded again.

exercises.question: Why does going through a list in order tend to be faster than visiting its items in a random order?
exercises.answer: Spatial locality. The cache brings in nearby items, so the next one is likely already there.

exercises.question: What's the average access time if the hit rate is 99%, the cache is 1 ns, and misses take 100 ns?

summary: Fast memory is small and costly, so computers use levels: registers, caches, RAM, then storage.
A cache holds copies of what's likely to be needed. A hit is fast, and a miss goes further away.
Caches work because of locality: things used now, and things nearby, get used again soon.
Average time = hit rate x cache time + miss rate x miss time.
Copies can go stale, and caches leave traces.

lessons.title: Find a file and read its location
lessons.source: Microsoft Support · File Explorer in Windows
lessons.goal: Read and write a full Windows file path, recognise a file by its extension, and set up one folder system for both schools that you can always find your way around.
lessons.why: You will hold course material from two universities, assignments, datasets and code for years. Losing a file before a NOUN deadline costs real marks. Paths also come straight back in programming, where a program opens files by path, and in security, where a fake extension is a classic trick. This skill looks small, and it is used every day of the degree.

blocks.text: A **file** is one named item of stored information: a PDF, a photo, a program. A **folder** (also called a directory) holds files and other folders. Folders inside folders form a tree.
A **path** is the exact address of an item in that tree. Read this one from left to right:

blocks.code: C:\Users\Ada\Documents\NOUN\COS101\tma1.docx

head: Part
Meaning
rows: The file: its name, then its extension

blocks.text: Two files can share a name as long as they sit in different folders, because their full paths differ. So `tma1.docx` in `NOUN\COS101` and `tma1.docx` in `NOUN\STA111` are completely separate. This is why the name alone never tells you which file you have.
Working on a copy by accident. You download `notes.pdf` twice, get `notes (1).pdf`, edit one and submit the other. Before you submit anything, check the full path of the exact file you are uploading.

blocks.question: What is the folder directly containing this file: `C:\Users\Ada\Documents\UNIPORT\STA112\week3.xlsx`?
blocks.answer: `STA112`. The last part is the file itself, and the part just before it is its parent folder.

blocks.text: Press **Windows key + E** to open File Explorer. The address bar at the top shows where you are. Each part is a button that jumps back to that level. Click the empty space in the address bar and it shows the full path as text, ready to copy.
Useful shortcuts:

head: Do this
To get this
rows: Click empty space in the address bar
See the full path as text
Ctrl + Shift + C on a selected file
Search this folder and the ones inside it

sections.title: Extensions tell Windows what a file is

blocks.text: The letters after the last dot are the **extension**. `.pdf` is a PDF, `.xlsx` an Excel workbook, `.py` Python code, `.exe` a program Windows can run. The extension tells Windows which app to open it with. It does not change what is inside. Renaming `photo.jpg` to `photo.pdf` does not make it a PDF, it just confuses Windows.
Windows hides common extensions by default. Turn them on, because it protects you. In File Explorer choose **View**, then **Show**, then **File name extensions**.

Attackers name a program `results.pdf.exe`. With extensions hidden, you may see only `results.pdf`, with the look of a document. It is a program, and opening it runs it. Keep extensions visible, and treat any `.exe`, `.bat`, `.scr` or `.js` file from a message or unknown site as dangerous until proven otherwise.

blocks.question: With extensions showing, you see `Course Outline.pdf.exe`. What kind of file is it really?
blocks.answer: A program. Only the last extension counts, and here it is `.exe`. The `.pdf` is just part of the name, probably there to fool you.

sections.title: A folder system for two schools

blocks.text: Decide your system once and use it for years. Keep it simple enough that you never need to think about where a file goes.

blocks.code:
Documents
  UNIPORT
    100 level
      STA111
        notes
        assignments
  NOUN
    100 level
      COS101
        material
        TMAs

blocks.text: Three rules make this work:

items: **One place per course.** Each course code gets one folder under its school.
**Names that sort and explain.** `2026-11-05 TMA1 draft.docx` tells you what it is and sorts by date, unlike `final final new.docx`.
**Keep UNIPORT and NOUN apart.** Credits and rules differ, and you must never submit one school's work to the other.

blocks.text: Plain names are safest. Letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens and dots all work, while Windows forbids `\ / : * ? " < > |` in file names. Later, when you write code, names without spaces will save you trouble.

A folder system is not a backup. If this laptop is stolen or its drive fails, every file in it goes too. Keep a second copy of anything you cannot replace on a separate drive. 4YOS backs up its own records, but not your other files.
Set up the real system you will use.

items: Press Windows key + E and turn on **File name extensions** under View, then Show.
In Documents, create `UNIPORT` and `NOUN`. Inside each, create a folder for at least one course you expect to take. Use your real course codes when you have them.
Move one real study file into the right folder. If you have none yet, create an empty text file named with today's date.
Click the address bar to see the full path, and press Ctrl + Shift + C on the file to copy it.
Close File Explorer, open it again and get back to the file using only the address bar.

rubric: File extensions are now visible on this laptop.

lessons.pack: Operating systems and networks
lessons.title: How Windows runs an app
lessons.source: Chris Terman · MIT OpenCourseWare · Computation Structures, Processes
lessons.goal: Explain what an operating system and its kernel do, tell a program from a process, and use Task Manager and a command to inspect real processes on this laptop.
lessons.why: Operating systems is a core 300-level course, and processes are its first big idea. In security it's everyday work: malware is a process, and analysts spend their days asking what's running, who started it, and what it's touching. Knowing how to look also solves plain problems, like finding what's slowing your laptop.

blocks.text: Watch how the operating system tracks a running program, saves its place, and lets another process use the same processor. The video uses registers and the memory management unit to explain the mechanism. Focus on what needs saving and why a timer helps. The reading walks through Windows Task Manager.
An **operating system** (OS) is the software that manages the hardware and gives programs a simpler way to use it. Two of its jobs are abstraction and arbitration.

**Abstraction** means hiding messy details behind a simple interface. A program doesn't need to know which brand of mouse or drive you have. It asks for "the next mouse movement" or "the file called notes.txt", and the OS and its **device drivers** deal with the specifics. A driver is software that lets the OS talk to one kind of device.

**Arbitration** means sharing limited hardware fairly among many programs. Several programs want the processor, memory and network at once, and the OS decides who gets what and keeps them from interfering with each other.
Kernel and operating environment

The **kernel** is the core of the OS. It runs with full authority over the hardware, while ordinary programs run with restricted rights in what's called **user mode**. To do anything sensitive, like reading a file, a program must ask the kernel using a **system call**, and the kernel can say no. This is the foundation of computer security.

In the strict sense the video uses, "operating system" means just the kernel. In everyday use, "Windows" includes the kernel plus all the tools and interfaces around it, which the video calls the **operating environment**. Both uses are common, so check which your lecturer means.
This distinction appears in every operating systems exam.

head: Program
Process
rows: In memory, with the processor's help
Can have many running at once

blocks.text: A good analogy: a recipe is a program, and cooking is the process. One recipe can be cooked by many people at the same time, each at a different step.
When you open Notepad, Windows reads `notepad.exe` from storage, sets up memory, and starts a process. Each process has:

items: A **PID**, or process ID, a number identifying it. PIDs can be reused after a process ends.
Its own **address space**, the memory it can see.
An identity, the **user** it runs as, which decides what it may access.
Open resources, such as files and network connections.
One or more **threads**, the separate paths of execution inside it.

blocks.text: Open a program twice and you may see two processes from one program file. Many modern apps, such as browsers, deliberately run as several processes, so that one crashed tab doesn't take down the rest.

Closing a window does not always end the process, and ending a process does not uninstall anything. An app may keep running in the background after you close it, and the program file stays on the drive after the process ends.

blocks.question: You delete a program's desktop shortcut. Does this uninstall the program, or end its running process?
blocks.answer: Neither. A shortcut is just a small file pointing to the program. The program file and any running process are unaffected.

sections.title: How one processor runs many things

blocks.text: A laptop might have hundreds of processes and only a handful of cores. The **scheduler** is the part of the kernel that gives each thread short turns on a core, switching so rapidly that everything seems to run at once. The switch itself is called a **context switch**.
A process is mostly in one of three states.

head: State
Meaning
rows: Able to run, waiting for a turn
Waiting for something, such as a key press, or a disk or network read

blocks.text: This is why Notepad can sit open using almost no CPU. It's blocked until you press a key. It still occupies memory, though. High CPU use means it's doing work, and high memory use means it's holding a lot.

Processes are isolated, because each has its own address space. One program can't simply read another's memory, unless it uses an approved mechanism with enough rights. A crash in one usually doesn't take down the others. And each process runs as a user, so its access to files is limited by that user's rights.

That's why **running as an ordinary user rather than as an administrator** matters. A malicious program you run accidentally gets your rights. If those are administrator rights, it can do far more damage.

A process's name proves nothing. Malware can name itself `svchost.exe` or something similar. Name alone isn't evidence, and high CPU alone isn't evidence either, since it could be a legitimate update. An analyst checks further: where the file is located, who signed it and what it's connected to. And don't end processes you don't recognise, because some are essential to Windows and ending them can crash it.

**Task Manager**, opened with Ctrl + Shift + Esc, has a **Processes** view that groups by app and a **Details** view with one row per process, which shows the PID and user. In Details, you can right-click a column header and choose **Select columns** to add more.
From the command line, `tasklist` lists processes. Filter for one:

blocks.code: tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq notepad.exe"

blocks.text: Later, on Linux, you will use `ps` and `top` for the same job.
Look at processes on this laptop, and don't end anything you didn't start yourself.

items: Save your work, then open Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc, and go to **Details**.
Open Notepad from Start, and find `Notepad.exe`. Note that you found its PID, and note its CPU and memory.
Type some text, and watch CPU for a few seconds. Then stop typing and watch again.
Open a second Notepad window. See whether a new process appears, or the same one grows. Modern Notepad may reuse a process, so report what you actually see.
Open Command Prompt: press the Windows key, type `cmd` and press Enter. Type or paste the command, then press Enter. Use the command below, and compare the result with Task Manager.
Close Notepad normally, and check again. Then explain why you can still open it from Start.

blocks.text: Keep your account name out of your answer.

rubric: I found a real process and its PID on this laptop, and reported what I saw.
I compared CPU use while typing with CPU use while idle.
I can explain why the program remains after the process ends.

exercises.question: Chrome is one program, and Task Manager shows many Chrome rows in Details. Why?
exercises.answer: Chrome deliberately runs several processes, for tabs and tasks, so that one crash or compromise is contained. It's one program and many processes.

exercises.question: A process uses 0% CPU and 400 MB of memory. Is it broken?
exercises.answer: Not necessarily. It's probably waiting for something. It holds memory without using the processor.

exercises.question: Your friend sees a process named `svchost.exe` using lots of CPU and wants to delete it. What should they do instead?
exercises.answer: Not delete or end it based on name and CPU alone. `svchost.exe` is a normal Windows host for services. Find out which service it's running and where the file is located first.

summary: The OS provides abstraction, and arbitrates access to shared hardware.
The kernel has full authority. Programs ask it through system calls.
A program is a stored file, and a process is that program running, with its own PID, memory and identity.
The scheduler gives threads turns on the cores. A waiting process uses memory but almost no CPU.
A process's name proves nothing. Don't end what you don't understand.

lessons.pack: Operating systems and networks
lessons.title: See who can use a file
lessons.source: Mike Murphy · Coastal Carolina University · Filesystems
lessons.goal: Explain what a filesystem stores besides your data, read a file's Windows permissions, and pick the least access that lets a task be done.
lessons.why: Access control is the most common security control in the world, and getting it wrong causes many real breaches. Wrong sharing settings expose private data with no hacking at all. In forensics at NOUN, file metadata such as timestamps becomes evidence. And when you run a web server or database later, the first question is always who can read and write what.

blocks.text: The video is about filesystems: how they organise a drive, and the metadata they keep, including owners and permissions. It mentions permissions only briefly, so the rules for reading and choosing them come from this lesson.

A storage device on its own is a huge run of numbered blocks with no structure. Before use, it's divided into **partitions**, and each is given a **filesystem**. The filesystem is the data structure that turns those blocks into named files in folders, so that data can be found and stored. Windows normally uses **NTFS** on its main drive. USB sticks often use **FAT32** or **exFAT**, and Linux commonly uses **ext4**.
Along with a file's contents, the filesystem keeps **metadata**.

head: Metadata
Tells you
Why it matters
rows: When its contents were last written
When it was last read, if recorded

blocks.text: So a file's name isn't inside the file. It's in the filesystem's records. That's why renaming a file leaves its bytes unchanged, and why it doesn't change a SHA-256 hash, which you'll see in another lesson.

Timestamps are evidence, but imperfect. Copying a file typically gives the copy a new created time, while keeping the modified time. So a file can appear to have been modified before it was created. An investigator needs to know these rules before relying on them. They can also be altered deliberately.

Permissions are only possible if the filesystem stores them. NTFS and ext4 do. FAT32 and exFAT don't, so anyone who plugs in that USB stick can read everything on it, regardless of what your PC's accounts are.

blocks.question: You copy a confidential file from your NTFS drive onto an exFAT USB stick. What happens to its permissions?
blocks.answer: They're lost, because exFAT can't store them. Anyone with the stick can open it. Encrypt it if it matters.

blocks.text: A path tells Windows **where** a file is. Permissions decide **whether** you may use it. Knowing a file's location gives you no access to it.
When a process tries to open a file, Windows compares two things:

items: The process's **identity**: the user it runs as, and all that user's groups.
The file's **access control list**, or ACL: a list of entries, each saying a user or group is allowed or denied certain actions.

blocks.text: So access mainly depends on who is asking, and not on which program is asking. If you run a malicious program, it can read anything you can.
The standard NTFS permissions

head: Permission
Lets you
Includes
rows: Also run it, if it's a program
Everything, including changing permissions and taking ownership

blocks.text: A few rules explain most of what you'll see.

items: **Inheritance.** Files normally take their permissions from their parent folder. Greyed-out ticks in the Security tab show inherited entries.
**Groups add up.** Your effective access combines entries for you and for all your groups.
**Deny beats allow**, in general, when entries conflict at the same level.
**Administrators can take ownership**, so permissions don't protect you against an administrator of that machine.

**Permissions only apply while the OS is enforcing them.** Someone who removes your drive and reads it from another system is not bound by Windows' checks. This is why stolen laptops need **encryption**, such as BitLocker.

blocks.text: The **principle of least privilege** says that a person or process should get only the access needed for its task, for only as long as it's needed.
Worked example: choose the permission

head: Task
Least access
Why not more
rows: Modify would let them change or delete it, by accident or otherwise
A teammate edits a shared document
Full control would let them change who else has access
Read on the sources, Write on its destination
It doesn't need to change the originals
A daily-use account on your laptop
Administrator rights would be given to anything you run

blocks.text: Least privilege doesn't stop an attack. It limits how much harm one can do, so malware running under a limited account can reach far less than under an administrator's.
Solving "access denied" by giving **Everyone** Full control. It works instantly, and it removes the protection for all accounts. Find which identity needs which right, and give only that.
The same idea applies to shared links. "Anyone with the link can edit" on a cloud document is a permission decision, and a common source of real data leaks.
**In File Explorer:** right-click a file, then **Properties**, then the **Security** tab. Select a group or user above to see their permissions below.
**At the command line:** `icacls` shows the ACL.

blocks.code: icacls "C:\Users\Ada\Documents\notes.txt"

C:\Users\Ada\Documents\notes.txt NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
                                 BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
                                 DESKTOP-1\Ada:(I)(F)

blocks.text: So the above says SYSTEM, Administrators and Ada each have inherited Full control. This is the normal layout for a file in your own documents. `SYSTEM` is the account Windows itself runs as.
Used with no options other than a path, `icacls` only reads. Options like `/grant` and `/reset` change permissions, and a wrong one can lock you out, so leave those for later and for test files.
Read, but don't change. Use a non-sensitive file you own, in a local folder.

items: Right-click the file, open **Properties**, then the **Security** tab. If there's no Security tab, it's probably on exFAT or FAT32, so pick a file on drive C.
Click each listed group or user, and note the permissions they hold. Are they inherited?

Open Command Prompt: press the Windows key, type `cmd` and press Enter. Type or paste the command, then press Enter. In File Explorer, click the file and press Ctrl + Shift + C to copy its path with its quotes. Then replace all of `"PASTE THE FILE PATH HERE"` with it, including those quotes, so that the path has only one pair. Match what you see to what the Security tab showed.
Decode one line using the table in the lesson.
Now imagine a reviewer who needs only to read this file. What would you give them, and what would you avoid giving?

blocks.text: Describe the entries by role, such as "my account" or "a system group". Keep your account name and path out of your answer. Leave the rules as you found them.

rubric: I read real permissions in both the Security tab and `icacls`, and matched them.
I decoded a real line, including the inherited marker.
I changed nothing, and I chose the least access for the imagined reviewer.

exercises.question: In `icacls` output, you see `BUILTIN\Users:(RX)`. What can the Users group do?
exercises.answer: Read the file and run it if it's a program. It can't change it.

exercises.question: You know the full path of a file holding someone else's exam script. Does knowing the path let you read it?
exercises.answer: No. The path says where it is. Whether you can read it depends on the permissions and your identity.

exercises.question: Someone with your stolen laptop boots it from a USB stick running Linux. Do your NTFS permissions stop them reading your files?
exercises.answer: No. Permissions are enforced by the running OS, and they're now running a different one. Drive encryption is what protects you here.

summary: A filesystem turns raw blocks into named files, and stores metadata beside them.
Permissions depend on the identity of the requesting process, not on the path or the program.
NTFS stores permissions. FAT32 and exFAT don't.
Least privilege means giving only the access a task needs. Never fix errors by giving Everyone Full control.
Permissions don't protect against a stolen drive. That takes encryption.

lessons.title: What happens when you press the power button
lessons.source: Microsoft Learn · Secure the Windows boot process
lessons.goal: Trace a computer from the power button to your desktop, name what each stage does, and use what you know to diagnose a laptop that won't start.
lessons.why: This pulls the unit together: firmware, memory, storage and the operating system, working in order. When a laptop won't start, knowing the stages tells you where it failed, and that often saves money on repairs. Boot security matters as well, because malware that gets in before the operating system is very hard to remove.

blocks.text: This lesson has no lecture, because I didn't find a free segment that I've confirmed teaches this well. The writing covers it fully.

The operating system is stored on the drive. Programs run from memory. But when the power comes on, memory is empty, so what loads the operating system? Starting a computer solves this in small steps, each loading something bigger. It's called **booting**, from the old phrase "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps".

head: Stage
What runs
What it does
Stored in
rows: Supplies stable power, and starts the processor
Starts at a fixed address, tests hardware, finds a boot drive
Finds and loads the operating system
Takes control of memory and the processor, and loads drivers

blocks.text: Firmware

When the power stabilises, the processor begins at one fixed address. This points to **firmware** on a chip, which keeps its contents without power. Older computers used **BIOS**, and modern ones use **UEFI**.

The firmware first runs a **power-on self-test** (POST), checking that key parts such as the memory work. Then it follows its **boot order**, the list of drives to try, looking for a boot loader. You reach its settings by pressing a key such as F2, F10, F12 or Del at startup, and it varies by maker.
Boot loader and kernel

The **boot loader** is a small program whose only job is to load the operating system. It copies the **kernel** into RAM, and hands over control. The kernel then takes charge of memory and the processor, and loads the drivers it needs to reach devices. Now the system can use the hardware through its layers.
Services and you
The kernel starts background programs, called **services** on Windows, for networking, updates, printing and security. Then comes the sign-in screen. After you sign in, **startup apps** run.

Thinking that a laptop gets slow to start because it's old. Often it's too many startup apps. Task Manager's **Startup apps** tab shows them, and you can disable ones you don't need. Don't disable what you don't recognise before checking what it does.

blocks.question: Your laptop shows the maker's logo, then a message "No bootable device". Which stage failed?
blocks.answer: The firmware ran, but it couldn't find a boot loader. So the drive may have failed, or the boot order may be wrong.

blocks.text: Windows has a feature called **Fast Startup**, on by default on many laptops. A **shut down** saves part of the system's state to the drive, in order to start faster next time. So the kernel isn't fully reloaded. A **Restart** does start fresh.
So, if IT support tells you to restart to fix a problem, choose **Restart** and not Shut down.

**Sleep** keeps RAM powered, so it wakes in seconds and uses a little battery. **Hibernate** copies memory to the drive and powers off, so it survives a flat battery, and takes longer. That's the memory lesson in action: RAM needs power, and storage doesn't.

sections.title: Diagnosing a laptop that won't start

blocks.text: Use the stages to narrow it down. Work from the first stage to the last.

head: What you see
Stage reached
What to try first
rows: Lights or fan, with a blank screen
Hold the power button 15 seconds, then try again. Check memory or the screen, which may need a technician
Windows logo, then a repeated failure
Blue screen with an error code
Note the code. Undo a recent driver or update

blocks.text: **Safe Mode** starts Windows with only the minimum set of drivers and services. If a problem disappears there, something you've added is the likely cause. It's a good test of which layer is to blame.
Before attempting repairs on a laptop that holds your only copies, remember your backups. A failing drive can get worse with every attempt, so copying your data comes first.

Malware that loads before the operating system can hide from everything that runs after it. A **rootkit** at this level is a serious problem. Modern computers defend themselves with a chain of checks.

head: Protection
What it does
rows: Firmware only runs boot loaders signed by a trusted key
Windows checks each of its parts before loading it
A security chip that holds keys, and records what was loaded
Encrypts the drive, using a key that the TPM can release only if the boot looks untampered

blocks.text: Each stage checks the next before handing over. That's called a **chain of trust**. A **digital signature** here is a maker's mark that software can check, and that can't be forged without the maker's secret key.

Someone with physical access can try to boot your laptop from a USB stick and read an unencrypted drive, without needing your Windows password. That's why drive encryption matters. Don't turn off Secure Boot or change firmware settings because a website or stranger tells you to. Keep your BitLocker recovery key stored somewhere safe and separate, because without it, you can be locked out of your own data.
Look only, and change nothing in the firmware.

items: Open Task Manager with **Ctrl + Shift + Esc**, and go to **Performance**, then **CPU**. Note the **Up time**. Does it surprise you? If you normally use Shut down, Fast Startup may explain a long uptime.
In Task Manager, open **Startup apps**. List the apps set to Enabled, and their startup impact. Choose one you might disable, and say why. You may disable it only if you're sure what it does.
Press the Windows key, type `system information`, and open it. Find **BIOS Mode** (UEFI or Legacy) and **Secure Boot State**.
Choose **Restart** from the Start menu after saving your work. Time how long it takes to reach the sign-in screen, and watch the stages go by.
In your own words, write the stages from power on to desktop. Then write where you'd look first if this laptop showed "No bootable device".

rubric: I found my real uptime, startup apps, BIOS mode and Secure Boot state.
I wrote the stages in order, from memory.
I can use the stages to say where to start looking for a fault.

exercises.question: Put in order: kernel loads, POST runs, boot loader runs, you sign in.
exercises.answer: POST runs, boot loader runs, kernel loads, you sign in.

exercises.question: Why is firmware stored on a chip, and not on the drive?
exercises.answer: Something has to run first, before any drive can be read, and memory is empty at power on.

exercises.question: A problem disappears when you start in Safe Mode. What does this suggest?
exercises.answer: Something beyond the minimum set, such as an added driver, service or startup app, is the likely cause.

exercises.question: Your laptop has a flat battery while hibernated. Have you lost your open work?
exercises.answer: Usually not, because hibernate saved memory to the drive. Sleep would be riskier, as it relies on RAM staying powered.

summary: Booting goes: power, firmware, boot loader, kernel, services, sign-in, desktop.
Firmware sits on a chip, because memory is empty at power on.
Windows' Shut down may not fully reload the system, while Restart does.
Use the stage that a fault reaches to decide what to check first.
Secure Boot, the TPM and BitLocker build a chain of trust. Keep your recovery key safe.

lessons.pack: How Computers Work · Computers talking
lessons.title: What a network is
lessons.source: Harvard CS50's Understanding Technology · Internet
lessons.goal: Say what a network and the internet are, explain why data travels in packets, name the main protocols and layers, and identify the devices that connect your laptop to the world.
lessons.why: A computer on its own is only part of the story. Nearly everything you do now crosses a network, and every later security topic assumes you understand how. This lesson gives you the big picture that the next two lessons fill in with addresses, routers, names and encryption.

blocks.text: This lesson has no lecture of its own. The next two lessons have clips from the Internet and Securing Systems lectures, and the full Internet lecture is linked below.
A **network** is two or more computers connected so that they can exchange data. Sizes vary.

head: Type
Stands for
Covers
Example
rows: Your phone and earbuds, over Bluetooth

blocks.text: The **internet** is a worldwide network of networks. No single company owns it. Thousands of networks, run by **internet service providers** (ISPs), universities and companies, agree to connect and to carry each other's traffic. The **web** is just one service that runs on it, alongside email, video calls and more.

Physically, it's mostly cables. Much international traffic travels through fibre-optic cables on the sea floor, and several land in Lagos. That's why a cable fault can slow the internet across a whole region. Your phone's "wireless" connection only goes wirelessly as far as the nearest mast, and from there it's mostly cable.

head: Device
Job
rows: The part of your laptop that connects it to a network
Connects wireless devices to the LAN
Connects different networks, and passes traffic toward its destination

blocks.text: A home "router" box usually does all of these jobs at once. A phone's hotspot does too, and it reaches the internet through mobile data.
Client and server

Most internet services work on the **client-server** model. A **client** asks, and a **server** answers. Your browser is a client. A **server** is simply a computer, or a program on it, that waits for requests. Other systems are **peer-to-peer**, where machines exchange directly with each other.

Data doesn't travel as one long stream. It's cut into small pieces called **packets**, each carrying a header with where it's from and where it's going. Think of sending a book by post, one page per envelope, with the page numbers marked.

head: Benefit
Why
rows: Many people's packets can share one line, taking turns
If a route fails, later packets can take another
Only lost packets need resending, not the whole file

blocks.text: This is called **packet switching**. It's a big part of why the internet was able to grow so large. Packets from one file may travel different routes and arrive out of order, and the receiver puts them back together.
Speed: bandwidth and latency

head: Word
Meaning
Comparison
rows: How much data per second, in bits per second
How long one packet takes, in milliseconds

blocks.text: They are different. A connection can have high bandwidth and high latency: a big download finishes fine, and a video call still lags.

Thinking "slow internet" always means low bandwidth. If web pages take time to start loading and calls lag, but big downloads are fast once started, latency is the likelier problem. More bandwidth won't fix that.

A **protocol** is an agreed set of rules for communicating, just as a phone call has rules: you say hello, take turns, and say goodbye. Computers from different makers can only talk because they follow the same protocols.

head: Protocol
Job
rows: Addresses packets, and gets them across networks. It doesn't promise delivery
Makes a reliable connection: numbers packets, resends lost ones, puts them in order
Sends quickly with no guarantees, and suits live calls and games

blocks.text: Layers
Networking is organised in layers, as software is. Each one only deals with its own job, and relies on the layer below.

head: TCP/IP layer
Job
Examples
rows: Reliable or quick delivery between programs
Moving data over one physical connection

blocks.text: Exams and courses also use the seven-layer **OSI model**. It splits these up more finely, and it's mainly used as a teaching and reference model. Learn it when your networking course reaches it.
Worked example: layers as envelopes
You request a web page. Each layer wraps the data with its own header, as with envelopes inside envelopes.

blocks.code: [ Link header [ IP header [ TCP header [ HTTP request ] ] ] ]

blocks.text: Routers read the IP header to choose the next hop. Only the destination's TCP and HTTP layers deal with what's inside. With HTTPS, the part inside is encrypted, which is how a router can forward a packet without being able to read it.

blocks.question: A live video call uses UDP for its sound. Why not TCP?
blocks.answer: TCP would stop to resend lost packets, and the delay would be worse than a tiny gap in the sound. Late data is useless in a live call.

blocks.text: Anyone between you and the destination could potentially see unencrypted traffic, including whoever runs a public Wi-Fi. Prefer HTTPS sites, and avoid banking on public Wi-Fi if you can use your mobile data. A tool such as Wireshark can capture traffic, and you should only use it on networks you own or have permission to monitor. Capturing other people's traffic without permission can be a crime.

items: Draw your own network on paper: this laptop, the Wi-Fi or hotspot it connects to, and everything else you know of on it. Mark where it joins your provider, and label each link wired or wireless.
Press the Windows key, type `cmd`, and press Enter. Run the command below. It sends a small test to a public address. Note the time values, in milliseconds. That's your latency.
Try it on two different connections if you can, or at two different times of day. Compare them.
Use your data app, or a speed test you trust, to find your bandwidth, if data allows. Say which you'd improve first for video calls, and for big downloads.
List three things you did online today, and name which protocol or service each one used, such as HTTPS or DNS.

blocks.text: If you're offline, note what happens, and explain which step failed.

rubric: I drew my real network, and marked what's wired and wireless.
I measured real latency.
I can explain the difference between bandwidth and latency in my own words.

exercises.question: Is your hostel's Wi-Fi a LAN or a WAN?
exercises.answer: A LAN. It covers one building or site.

exercises.question: What's the difference between the internet and the web?
exercises.answer: The internet is the worldwide network of networks. The web is pages carried on it, one service among many.

exercises.question: A 1 GB file is split into packets, and a few get lost. What happens under TCP?

lessons.goal: Read your network settings with `ipconfig`, use a subnet mask to decide if an address is local, and explain how a packet reaches a server through your default gateway and routers.
lessons.why: Nothing in cybersecurity makes sense without this. NOUN's networking course starts here, and packet captures, firewalls, and attack and defence all assume you can read addresses and follow a route. It's also how you diagnose real problems, such as whether a failure is your Wi-Fi, your router or the wider internet. You already have the binary to understand it.

blocks.text: The video starts as David Malan reads a Mac's network settings, then shows the Windows equivalent and explains routers and hops. Subnet calculation and tools like `ping` are added in this lesson.

Data crosses a network in small chunks called **packets**. A large download becomes many thousands of them. Each carries a header with its source and destination addresses, like the writing on an envelope.

An **IPv4 address** is 32 bits written as four numbers from 0 to 255, such as `192.168.1.10`. Each number is one byte, which you saw in the binary lesson. There are about 4.3 billion such addresses, which isn't enough for today's devices, so **IPv6** uses 128 bits, written like `2001:db8::1`. You will see both.
An address belongs to a **network interface**, such as Wi-Fi or Ethernet, and not really to the computer. A laptop on Wi-Fi and Ethernet has two.
Private and public addresses
Certain ranges are reserved for private networks, under the standard RFC 1918.

These addresses don't work on the public internet, and millions of networks reuse them. Your router uses **NAT**, or network address translation, to share one public address among your devices. So the address on your laptop isn't the address that websites see. Mobile networks in particular often share one public address among many customers.

`127.0.0.1` is **loopback**: it always means this computer itself. An address starting `169.254` usually means your computer tried to get an address automatically and failed, which is a useful clue that something's wrong with the network or the router.
How you get an address
On most networks, **DHCP** automatically gives your device four things when it connects, and they're the four to know:

head: Setting
Purpose
rows: Identifies your interface on this network
The router to send everything else to
Turns names into addresses, covered next lesson

blocks.text: Before sending, your computer must decide if the destination is on the same local network. The **subnet mask** answers this. Where the mask has 1 bits, the address must match for two devices to be on the same network.

The most common mask is `255.255.255.0`. In binary that's 24 ones followed by 8 zeros, which is why it's also written `/24`. For that mask, the first three numbers name the network, and the last names the device.
Worked example: local or not?
Your address is `192.168.1.10`, and the mask is `255.255.255.0`.

Masks don't have to fall on these neat boundaries. The computer actually does a bitwise AND of the address and the mask, and compares the results. With `/26`, for instance, the last byte is split, which you will calculate in the networking course. Python's standard library can check it for you:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress
network = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24")
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.25") in network)
print(ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.2.25") in network)
print(network.netmask)
print(network.num_addresses)

blocks.question: Your address is `10.0.1.34`, with mask `255.255.255.0`. Is `10.0.1.1` local? What about `10.0.2.1`?
blocks.answer: `10.0.1.1` is local, since the first three numbers match. `10.0.2.1` is not, so it goes via the gateway.

blocks.text: A **router** connects networks. Your **default gateway** is the router on your local network that takes everything not local. It's the exit door, and it must be on your local network, otherwise your computer couldn't reach it.

A router keeps a **routing table**, which is essentially a list of address prefixes and where to send them next. As the video says, it picks a direction and passes the packet to the **next hop**. No router knows the entire path. Each only knows a better next step, and that's enough. Each step is a **hop**.
A packet's journey
Say your laptop at `192.168.1.10` sends a packet to a web server at a public address.

items: **Your laptop** sees the destination isn't local, so it sends the packet to the gateway.
**Your home router** applies NAT, replacing your private source address with its public one, and sends it to your provider.
**Your provider's routers** pass it on, following their tables.
**Routers across the internet** carry it hop by hop, possibly through several countries.
**The server** receives it and replies to the public address.
**Your router** recognises the reply and passes it back to your private address.

blocks.text: Each packet has a **time to live** value, reduced at every hop, and when it reaches zero, the packet is dropped. This stops packets from circling forever. Packets may also get lost, or arrive out of order, and higher-level protocols such as TCP deal with that.

head: Command
What it tells you
rows: Also your DNS servers and whether DHCP is on
Whether you can reach an address, and the round-trip time in milliseconds

blocks.text: `ping` makes a good troubleshooting ladder. Ping your gateway. If that fails, the problem's between you and your router. If it works but a public address fails, the problem's beyond your router. If an address works but a website's name doesn't, suspect DNS.
A failed ping doesn't prove a machine is off, because many systems block ping on purpose. Treat it as a clue, not proof.
An IP address tells you where to send data, not who someone is or whether to trust them.

Private addresses aren't protection in themselves. Other devices on the same Wi-Fi can often reach yours, depending on the firewall. On unfamiliar networks, such as a campus or café, choose the **Public network** profile in Windows, which is more restrictive. Your IP addresses are not secret, but they do identify your network, so keep them out of screenshots and notes you share. Only run `ping` and `tracert` as normal, and don't scan networks you don't own. Scanning without permission can break school rules, or the law.
Read your own settings. Change nothing, and keep actual addresses out of your answer, since they identify your network.

items: Open Command Prompt: press the Windows key, type `cmd` and press Enter. Type or paste the command, then press Enter. Use the command below. Find the adapter you're actually using, and ignore any marked Media disconnected.
Find its IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask and Default Gateway. If any is missing, record that.
Is your address private? Which range is it in? Use the mask to say which part names the network.
Run `ping` with your gateway's address, then `ping 8.8.8.8`. Note whether each worked and the rough times, and which was faster and why.
Run `tracert 8.8.8.8`. Count the hops.

blocks.text: Explain in your own words where a packet goes first when you open a website, and why. If you're offline, say what you saw and what you'd expect when connected.

rubric: I found my real interface and read its address, mask and gateway.

exercises.question: Is `172.20.5.1` a private address? And is `172.40.5.1`?
exercises.answer: `172.20.5.1` is, as it's within 172.16 to 172.31. `172.40.5.1` is not, so it's public.

exercises.question: Your computer shows `169.254.33.7`. What does that suggest?
exercises.answer: It didn't get an address from DHCP. Check the Wi-Fi connection or the router.

exercises.question: Pinging your gateway works, but `ping 8.8.8.8` doesn't. Where is the problem likely to be?
exercises.answer: Beyond your router: the router's link to your provider, your data, or the provider itself.

exercises.question: A `/24` network has 256 addresses. How many does a `/25` have, and why?
exercises.answer: 128. One more network bit leaves 7 bits for devices, and 2^7 is 128. A `/24` has 2^8.

summary: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four bytes. Private ranges are reused behind NAT.
DHCP gives you an address, mask, gateway and DNS server.
The mask decides what's local. Local traffic goes direct, and everything else goes to the default gateway.
Routers pass packets hop by hop. None knows the whole path.
Ping your gateway, then a public address, then a name, to find where a problem is.

lessons.source: Eric Twark · Harvard CS50's Computer Science for Business · Week 5, Implementing the Internet
lessons.goal: Break a URL into its parts, follow a request through DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP, and say exactly what the padlock proves and what it doesn't.
lessons.why: Most scams you'll ever study rest on people misreading a web address, or believing the padlock means a site is honest. Your planned channel is built around this. It's also core networking, and it's everyday work for a security analyst. Being able to read a hostname correctly protects your own money and accounts today.

blocks.text: Follow a browser request from the address bar through DNS, an encrypted HTTPS connection and the server's response. The written lesson explains how TLS verifies the site's identity and what the padlock can tell you.

blocks.code: https://portal.example.edu.ng:443/results/view?session=2026#top

head: Part
Example
Meaning
rows: How to talk to the server
Which server, the part to check
Which service on that server, usually hidden
A place in the page, not sent to the server

blocks.text: Hostnames read **from the right**. In `portal.example.edu.ng`, `ng` is the top-level domain, `edu.ng` is a level under it, `example.edu.ng` is the registered domain, and `portal` is a subdomain the owner created. The owner of `example.edu.ng` can create any subdomain they want. That's the key to reading scam links.
Worked example: who controls this?

head: Link
Registered domain
Who really controls it
rows: The same. The bank's name is just in the path

blocks.text: Looking for the bank's name somewhere in the link. Its presence means nothing. Look only at what sits immediately before the end of the hostname, the first `/` closes it.

blocks.question: Who controls `https://login.nou.edu.ng.account-verify.com/start`?
blocks.answer: Whoever registered `account-verify.com`. Reading from the right, that's the registered domain, and everything before it is a subdomain they chose.

blocks.text: Computers route by IP address, not by name. The **Domain Name System** is a huge distributed database that maps names to addresses. It's often compared to a phone book, but no single place holds all of it.

items: Your browser checks its cache, and Windows checks its own.
If it isn't there, your computer asks its **DNS resolver**, usually run by your provider or router, or chosen by you.
If the resolver doesn't have it cached, it asks a **root server**, which refers it to the servers for `.ng` or `.com`.
Those refer it to the domain's **authoritative** server, which gives the actual answer.
The resolver returns the address, and everyone caches it for a time.

blocks.text: The two most common record types are **A** for an IPv4 address, and **AAAA** for an IPv6 address. There are also others, such as MX, for mail servers.

Standard DNS is sent unencrypted, so your provider and others on the path can see which names you look up, and traditionally its answers aren't verified. Newer options include DNS over HTTPS, which encrypts the lookups. Either way, a DNS answer only tells you **where to connect**, and nothing about whether to trust what's there.
Once your browser has an address:

items: **TCP** sets up a reliable connection to the server, normally on port 443 for HTTPS, or 80 for plain HTTP. A **port** identifies which service on the machine you want.
**TLS** sets up encryption, and checks the server's certificate.
**HTTP** carries the actual request and response. The browser asks for a path, as in `GET /results/view`, and the server returns a **status code** and the content.

blocks.text: **HTTPS** is simply HTTP running inside TLS.
TLS provides three things.

head: Property
What it means
CIA link
rows: People on the path can't read the contents
People on the path can't alter the contents unnoticed
The server proves it holds the certificate for that hostname

blocks.text: Encryption here uses a pair of matching keys: a **public key** anyone may have, and a **private key** its owner keeps secret. A **digital signature** is a mark made with a private key, which anyone can check with the public key, and which can't be forged without it. As the video explains, the server has a **certificate**: a public key, for a hostname, signed by a **certificate authority** (CA). Your browser and operating system ship with a list of CAs they trust. Your browser checks that the certificate chain leads to a trusted CA, that it covers the exact hostname, and that it's within its dates. Only then does it use it.

Note what stays visible, as the video's envelope analogy shows. The source and destination IP addresses are on the outside, and observers can usually also see the hostname being connected to. They can't see the path, the page contents or what you type.
This is the most important part of this lesson. A valid certificate means **"this connection is encrypted, and you're talking to this hostname"**. It doesn't mean the site is honest.

head: The padlock proves
The padlock doesn't prove
rows: That the site belongs to who it says
Nobody on the path can read or alter it
That the people running it are honest

blocks.text: Certificates for ordinary domains are issued automatically, often for free, to anybody who can show they control a domain. Criminals get them routinely for lookalike sites. So `https://mybank-secure-login.net` can have a perfectly valid certificate. The encryption works perfectly, and it protects your password all the way to the thief.

For anything that matters, such as your bank, your school portal or your email, don't follow links from messages. Type the address yourself or use a bookmark you've made. If your browser shows a certificate warning, stop. Don't click through, and don't change security settings to make it go away. Check the address by another route. On public Wi-Fi, a warning can mean someone is interfering with your connection.
This needs no sign-in and no changes to any settings. If you're offline, do what you can, and say which steps you couldn't observe.

items: Open Command Prompt: press the Windows key, type `cmd` and press Enter. Type or paste the command, then press Enter. Use the command below. Identify the resolver's section and the answer's section. Note whether any addresses came back, and whether they were IPv4, IPv6 or both. Leave the resolver's address out of your notes.
Type `https://www.iana.org/` directly into your browser. Check the final hostname in the address bar, since it may have redirected you.
Click the icon to the left of the address, and find the connection and certificate information. Note who issued the certificate and when it expires.
Take any three links from messages or emails you've received, without opening them, and write the registered domain of each one. Don't include any private details.
Write one sentence on what the DNS lookup told you, and one on what the browser verified. Then write one thing that neither of them proved.

rubric: I ran a real lookup, and I can point to the resolver and the answer.
I found who issued a real certificate.
I worked out the registered domain of three real links, without opening them.

exercises.question: In `https://www.uniport.edu.ng.fees-pay.org/portal`, what's the registered domain?
exercises.answer: `fees-pay.org`. Everything before it is a subdomain, and `uniport.edu.ng` here means nothing.

exercises.question: A site shows a valid padlock, and asks for your BVN and card details to "unlock a grant". Does the padlock make it safe?
exercises.answer: No. It proves the connection is encrypted to that hostname. Anyone can get a certificate. The request itself is a warning sign.

exercises.question: `ping` by address works, but `ping` by name fails. Which step is broken?
exercises.answer: DNS. The network route is fine, but the name isn't being turned into an address.

exercises.question: Someone on the same Wi-Fi watches your HTTPS traffic. Can they see your password? Can they see which site you visited?
exercises.answer: Not the password or the page contents. They can see the server's address and usually the hostname.

summary: Read hostnames from the right. The registered domain is the name just before the public ending (`.com`, `.com.ng`, `.edu.ng`), together with that ending.
DNS turns a name into an address. It says where to connect, not whether to trust.
TCP connects, TLS secures, and HTTP carries the request. HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS.
TLS gives encryption, integrity and proof of the hostname.
The padlock doesn't mean a site is honest. Criminals have valid certificates too.

lessons.goal: Trace everything that happens from clicking a link to seeing the page, naming the hardware, software and network steps, and use that trace to find where a real problem lies.
lessons.why: This lesson joins up the entire course. "What happens when you open a web page?" is a classic job interview question, because a good answer proves that you understand the whole machine. You'll also use this skill constantly, because any real fault, from a slow site to a security incident, is found by knowing the chain and testing it link by link.

blocks.text: This is a practice lesson. It teaches nothing new, and has no lecture. It connects what you've already learned, so go back to earlier lessons if a step is unclear.
You click a link to `https://www.example.com/fees`. Here's what happens, with the unit where you learned it.

head: Step
What happens
Learned in
rows: The touchpad sends a signal, and a driver passes it to Windows
Windows tells the browser, a process with its own memory, that you clicked
The processor runs the browser's instructions, loop after loop of fetch, decode, execute
How a processor runs a program
The browser reads the URL, and checks its cache for this page
Why computers keep copies close by
It needs an address, so it checks caches, then asks a DNS resolver
From a website name to a secure connection
Your laptop compares the address with its subnet mask, and sees that it isn't local
Follow a packet off your network
The network interface sends the packet over Wi-Fi to the default gateway
Follow a packet off your network
Routers pass packets hop by hop, across cables
TCP connects, then TLS checks the certificate and sets up encryption
From a website name to a secure connection
The browser sends an HTTP request. The server replies with text, in many packets
The bytes are decoded as UTF-8 text
Images arrive compressed, and they're decompressed to pixels in RAM
How files get smaller, How pictures become numbers
The page is held in RAM, and some of it is cached on the drive
The graphics hardware sets each pixel's red, green and blue values
Gates and transistors, billions of them, did all of the above

blocks.text: All of this usually happens in under a few seconds.

blocks.question: At which steps could someone on the same public Wi-Fi see something, if the site used plain HTTP and not HTTPS?
blocks.answer: At the network steps, 7 to 10, they could read the request and reply. With HTTPS they'd still see the address and usually the hostname, but not the contents.

blocks.text: When something fails, don't guess. Work out which link in the chain broke. Each test should split the possibilities roughly in half.
Worked example: "the internet isn't working"

head: Test
If it works
If it fails
rows: The fault is with that site
Does another device work on this Wi-Fi?
It's the Wi-Fi or the provider
It's between the laptop and the router
It's the router, or beyond it

blocks.text: Worked example: a slow laptop

head: Clue from Task Manager
What it points to
rows: CPU near 100%, and one app at the top
Memory near full, with the disk busy too
RAM, and the page file being used
Disk at 100% and an old hard disk
All low, but the page is slow
Everything fine until a recent change

blocks.text: Always ask what changed recently, and write down what you tried. Change one thing at a time. These are the same habits you use in debugging code.
You should now be able to explain each of the following in about a minute, closed book, without jargon that you can't explain yourself. Say them aloud, or write them down.

head: Question
Check that you mention
rows: How does a computer add two numbers?
How does a letter get saved in a file?
Why does a laptop lose unsaved work in a power cut?
Encryption and the hostname, not honesty
Why is a second app open slower than expected?
RAM, cache, or the page file

blocks.text: Thinking that you know this because the table looks familiar. That's the illusion of knowing. Cover it up, explain it from memory, and only then check yourself.

This trace is also how defenders think. Each step is somewhere an attack could happen: a fake link at step 1, malware at step 2, a false DNS answer at step 5, a dishonest Wi-Fi at step 7. Learning the chain is how you learn to defend it. Only test systems you own or have written permission to test.
Follow a real click, and write up what you can actually observe.

items: Open a browser, and press **F12**, which opens its developer tools. Click the **Network** tab. Then type `https://www.iana.org/` in the address bar and press Enter.
In the list, click the first row. Find the status code, the remote address, and the content type. Note the size and time of the largest item in the list.
Reload with **Ctrl + R**. Which items now say they came from a cache? Compare the time and the amount transferred.
Click the padlock or site icon, and find who issued the certificate.
Open Task Manager, and find the browser's memory and CPU while the page loads.
Now write your own 15-step trace of that click, in your own words, closed book, including what you saw. Use the table to check it only after finishing.
Think of a real computer problem you've had. Write the tests that you'd run, in order, to find the broken link.

blocks.text: Keep your trace, as you'll use it in the course project.

rubric: I observed a real page load in the developer tools.
I wrote the trace from memory, before I checked it against the table.
I wrote an ordered set of tests for a real problem.

exercises.question: A page loads, but its images are missing. Which part of the chain would you suspect, and why not DNS for the main site?
exercises.answer: The main site's DNS, connection and HTML worked, since the page came. The images may come from another server or may have failed separately. Check the browser's message, or try opening one directly.

exercises.question: You open a spreadsheet you just closed, and it opens faster. Which idea explains this?
exercises.answer: Caching. Windows kept recently read parts of the file, and of the program, in RAM.

exercises.question: `ping 8.8.8.8` works, and `ping www.example.com` says it could not find the host. What's wrong?
exercises.answer: DNS. The route works, and the name lookup is failing.

exercises.question: Task Manager shows memory at 98%, disk activity high, and CPU at 20%. What's the most likely bottleneck?
exercises.answer: RAM. Windows is moving memory to the page file on the drive, which makes the disk busy.

exercises.question: Name a step in the journey that only exists because of an agreement rather than physics.
exercises.answer: Many do: UTF-8, HTTP, IP addresses and RGB are all agreed formats and protocols.

exercises.question: Why can your browser show a page without ever knowing the route that it took?
exercises.answer: Layers. The browser uses HTTP and TCP, and each router only knows the next hop.

summary: One click uses the whole machine: input, drivers, a process, the processor, cache, DNS, routing, TLS, HTTP, encoding, decompression, RAM and the screen.
To find a fault, test link by link, and choose tests that split the possibilities.
Ask what changed recently, and change one thing at a time.
Each step is also a possible point of attack, and a point to defend.
If you can explain it with the source closed, you know it.

The folder that a program is installed in
